1)stabilize soils on the site, 2)compete with annual grass and noxious weed establishment, 3)promote proper

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Objective(s)
1. Attain a density of one sagebrush seedling per 10m\xb2 in suitable areas. Conduct Aerial
Seeding Shrub Hoop monitoring.
2. Quantitative objectives were not tied to aerially seeded forb or grass germination and
survivorship; qualitatively the objective for these groups is to increase forb diversity and
establish sagebrush and cool season (early germinating) perennial grasses. Conduct
Aerial Seeding and Line Point Intercept monitoring and Site Assessments.

2021 Results: 
The objective of one sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata ssp. wyomingensis) seedling per 10m2 has not been met 5 or 10 years post-fire. Seeded sagebrush were uncommon across the burned area in both 2016 and 2021. In 2012, average sagebrush seedling density was less than 0.1 per 10m2, and only trace amounts (<2%) mature sagebrush were seen in 2013 but no seedlings were observed. In 2014 the entire area was surveyed for shrubs with a focus on areas most suitable for sagebrush seedling establishment in the south and east of the fire perimeter. Trace amounts of seedlings were observed in the eastern portion of the fire; none were seed in the southern portion. Sagebrush foliar cover from line point intercept was also trace; 1% in 2012, 0.7% in 2013 and 0.3% in 2014. Small patches of remnant shrubs were observed in the Center allotment in an area that had been both drill and aerially seeded.

Drill and aerially seeded cool season grass cover has not changed substantially between 2014 and 2021 based on qualitative site assessments. Seeded perennial forb species observed in 2012, 2013, 2014 and 2021 included alfalfa, Western yarrow, and Lewis’ flax. Sandberg bluegrass was a subdominant or minor component of the plant community at each plot monitored in 2021 except CP03. Few sagebrush seedlings were observed in suitable sites; therefore, the objective to establish sagebrush is not being met (See photos below).
Aerially seeded locations (including areas also drill seeded) were meeting the objective of cool season perennial grass establishment in 2012, 2013 and 2014. Although aerially seeded grass germination was low, particularly for sand dropseed, Sandberg bluegrass and historically seeded crested/Siberian wheatgrass have recovered. In 2014, site assessments indicated that perennial vegetation was the dominant cover and grasses were in good vigor over the majority of the seeded area; annuals were dominant cover at only three monitoring plots. Overall Sandberg bluegrass was the most abundant cover, other perennial grasses observed in subdominant (10-40%) or dominant composition were bottlebrush squirreltail, Snake River wheatgrass bluebunch wheatgrass. Small patches of existing sagebrush were present throughout. Where annuals were dominant, cheatgrass was the most common annual species and bare soil ranged from a quarter to half of the site.
Perennial forb diversity is also meeting the objective, and although abundance was low across the landscape this was expected because of the low seeding rates Table (8-8). Naturally occurring forbs including hawksbeard (Crepis sp.), phlox (Phlox sp.), globemallow (Sphaeralcea sp.), milkvetch (Astragalus sp.) and wild onion (Allium sp.) larkspur (Delphinium sp.), deathcamas (Zigadenus venosus), buckwheat (Eriogonum sp.), and dusty maiden (Chaenactis douglasii) were present in trace amounts.

Actual_Implementation:
Seed was purchased for BAR revegetation treatments on 8/28.

The seed lot that was purchased on 8/28 was sent to a certified seed laboratory for testing to meet BLM Standards (i.e., no Idaho noxious weeds and minimum 0.765 PLS).

- - - - - 2007 MonFund - - - - -

The aerial seeding was monitored during the 2007.

- - - - - 2008 MonFund - - - - -

The aerial seeding was monitored during the 2007 and 2008 field seasons.

Monitoring in 2008 consisted of 2 transects in chained and seeded areas, and 3 transects in drill-seeded areas and 3 transects in reference areas that were burned but not seeded (see Fig. 1). Each transect was 20 x 300 ft., thereby covering a total area of 6,000 ft. Big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata) plants were counted within transects. Yarrow, flax and penstemon were not monitored in 2008.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Monitoring conducted in the chained area showed that this area had the highest diversity of perennial grass species.  This area had very little crested wheatgrass present, however there was little present prior to the fire.  Monitoring showed that the aerial seeding objective was achieved at the excellent level. 

The transects that were conducted in the acres of the seeding, found the existing burned vegetation recovering, but found very little of the seeded species. However, it may be just too soon to tell how well this seeding will take. More monitoring will be done in 2008 and provide a better overall picture on results.

There were sage brush, white yarrow, Lewis flax, and Wasatch penstemon seedlings found through out the burn, although it is almost impossible to tell if they are natural or from the aerial seeding. This area will be monitored next year to assess the effectiveness of the aerial seeding.

Sagebrush seeding monitoring was done by reading sagebrush density belt transects at each of the eight previously established transect sites. A three hundred foot baseline tape was stretched at the site, and three transects were read at random points along the baseline. Each belt transect was three hundred feet long and 16 feet wide. One sagebrush plant was found in the burned, drill-seeded site in 2008. No other sagebrush plants were counted in reference, drill- or aerial-seeded sites (Table 1). The dominant and almost exclusive vegetation is crested wheatgrass. Clearly these aerial and drill-seeding methods are not effective and should be reviewed before further implementation at other sites.

Lessons learned:
The practice of chaining dead juniper trees was particularly devastating on soil structure and revegetation. Fig. 2 (below) shows an unchained area allowed to naturally recover. While damage from the burn is still apparent, reasonable revegetation compared with surrounding reference sites occurred. Chained areas (Figs. 3-6), although seeded with native vegetation, show lower levels of both native and exotic revegetation and often present large patches of bare ground (Figs. 3 and 4). In areas with gentle slopes, water runoff combined with disturbances from cattle have caused large gullies through the loose soil (Figs. 5 and 6).

Actual_Implementation: Sagebrush and yarrow were seeded to add vegetation structure and species richness to treated areas.  \r\nThe aerial wildlife seeding was completed in January via fixed wing through an aircraft rental agreement. The ground crew consisted of BLM helitack and a project inspector. AG Nav maps of the aerial seeding were completed for the project file.  Aerial seeding was monitored to ensure the correct seed mixture was dispersed over the target area at the specified rate.  A project inspector was present to ensure treatment met contract specifications.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

The Charleston Aerial Wildlife (High Elevation) Seeding was monitored at three separate locations. One was specifically established to monitor this treatment (CHWH – 01), one was established to monitor the Aerial Watershed Protection Seeding where it is overlapped by the Aerial Wildlife (High Elevation) Seeding (CHWS – 03), and one was established to monitor native release on a Mountain Ridge range site within the high elevation wildlife seeding (CHNR – 05). 

Monitoring Results: 
2007 – At CHWH – 01, Western Yarrow was present at a density near one and three-quarters plants square meter (exceeding the objective density of one plant per square meter), Mountain Big Sagebrush was recorded at a density approaching one-half plant per square meter.  At CHWS – 03, Western Yarrow appeared to increase to a density approaching three plants per square meter (well exceeding the objective density of one plant per square meter), Mountain Big Sagebrush was present at a density near one-third plant per square meter.  At CHNR – 05 neither Western Yarrow nor Mountain Big Sagebrush were recorded. 
2008 – At CHWH – 01, Western Yarrow appeared to decline in density by more than one plant per square meter, Mountain Big Sagebrush was not recorded.  At CHWS – 03, Western Yarrow maintained a density near two and one-half plants per square meter but Mountain Big Sagebrush was not recorded.  Fluctuations should be evaluated cautiously because individual quadrat frames are not absolutely repeatable from year to year along a paced transect.  At CHNR – 05 Western Yarrow was not recorded but Mountain Big Sagebrush approached a density of one-half plant per square meter. 
2009 – Monitoring plot CHNR – 05  was specifically established to monitor native release at the request of the Elko range staff and only monitored ESR treatments incidentally.  It was not re-read by ESR staff during the final year of monitoring.  
Western Yarrow exceeded the objective density of three plants per square meter at CHWS – 03 during the final year of monitoring.  Western Yarrow was observed in abundance in the areas surrounding CHWS – 03, visible in parallel whitish “stripes” across the upland landscape that indicated flight paths.  Since Western Yarrow was “double seeded” at the CHWS – 03 monitoring location (that is, seeded with both the Aerial Wildlife (high elevation) Seeding and the Aerial Watershed Protection Seeding that overlapped there,) an exact determination of which treatment provided the yarrow that was recorded cannot be made.  However, evidence of both seedings was clear where a slightly broader whitish stripe ran diagonally to the upland parallel stripes, down the middle of the V-shaped intermittent drainage seeded during the watershed protection treatment.  Western Yarrow was recorded at a moderate density exceeding one-third plant per square meter at CHWH – 01; Mountain Big Sagebrush was not recorded.  Success varied between monitoring locations and throughout the monitoring period.  The Charleston Aerial Wildlife (high elevation) Seeding may be considered partially successful based upon solely upon observations and recorded density for Western Yarrow at CHWS – 03.   Mountain Big Sagebrush was generally less successful, but was recorded at several locations at low-to-moderate density over the monitoring period, and fluctuations may result from absolute non-repeatability of individual quadrats along the paced transects used to monitor this treatment.

Implementation of the proposed action described in the Emergency Stabilization and Rehabilitation Plan DNA for the Charleston Complex will protect soils in the burned area, including preventing potential loss of soil due to wind and water erosion&* will reduce potential invasion and establishment of noxious weeds and cheatgrass&* will provide quality forage for livestock and wildlife&* and will facilitate meeting established standards and guidelines for livestock grazing.  

Exclusion of livestock grazing is necessary to allow seedling establishment, restore plant vigor and seed production, and to allow reestablishment of preferred species and to deter invasion of undesirable species.  The proposed fence will be constructed around the burn perimeter to keep grazing animals off the recovering burn to allow establishment of seeded and pre-fire vegetation species.  This temporary fencing will be used in conjunction with existing fences to protect the burn area from grazing. Objectives: The primary objective of the treatment is to seed watershed areas of the burn that are at highest risk for significant erosion and non-native species invasion. Watersheds are especially at risk as they generally had the greatest build up of vegetation pre-fire, causing the fire to burn hot and destroy all vegetation and species in the seedbank. \r\nEstablish three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in soil with consideration for site selection factors of soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and potential for seedling establishment. Planned_Implementation: Aerially seed approximately 10062 acres with a watershed protection mixture (\u201cCharleston Watershed Mix\u201d) of \u201cSherman\u201d Big Bluegrass, \u201cBannock\u201d Thickspike Wheatgrass, \u201cSecar\u201d Snake River Wheatgrass, and \u201cMagnar\u201d Basin Wildrye.\r\n\r\nAdd Western Yarrow and Basin Big Sagebrush to the watershed protection seed mixture (\u201cCharleston watershed mix\u201d) of native grasses.
Actual_Implementation:
Due to the availability of water and other resources necessary for regrowth, a mix of both native and non-native species (Snake River wheatgrass, Sherman big bluegrass, Magnar and trailhead Basin wild rye, Bluebunch wheatgrass, Siberian wheatgrass, Idaho Fescue, and Schwendimar and Bannock thickspike wheatgrass) was selected. Additional shrubs were added to the mix, and are discussed in the Burned Area Rehabilitation treatment monitoring section.

Implementation Monitoring:  
The aerial watershed protection seeding was completed during January via fixed wing through an aircraft rental agreement. The ground crew consisted of BLM helitack and a project inspector.  AG Nav maps of the aerial seeding were completed for the project file.  Aerial seeding was monitored to ensure the correct species seed mixture was dispersed over the targeted area at the specified rate. The project inspector ensured treatment met contract specifications.

BAR addition of western yarrow and sagebrush:
“Delar” Small Burnet may have been substituted for Western Yarrow at some indeterminate locations.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

The Charleston Aerial Watershed Protection Seeding was monitored at seven separate locations (CHWS – 01, CHWS – 02, CHWS – 03, CHWS – 04, CHWS – 05, CHWS – 06, CHWS – 07) specifically established to monitor this treatment on all range grazing allotments affected by the fire. 

Monitoring Results: 
2007 – Total seeded species density exceeded the objective density of three plants per square meter at all monitoring locations.  Thickspike Wheatgrass typically made the greatest contribution to total seeded species density.  Basin Wildrye was also very successful
2008 – Total seeded species density continued to exceed the objective density of three plants per square meter at CHWS – 01, CHWS – 02, CHWS – 03, and CHWS – 05, appearing to increase slightly at CHWS – 01 CHWS – 02, and CHWS – 03.  Total seeded species density appeared to decline at CHWS – 04, CHWS – 05, CHWS – 05, and CHWS – 07.  Thickspike Wheatgrass continued to make the greatest contribution to total seeded species density.  All other seeded species declined dramatically and were not recorded, except at CHWS – 04, where Basin Wildrye was recorded at moderate density.  Downward trend in seeded species at CHWS – 04 and CHWS – 05 appears unrelated to competition from native release Sandberg’s Bluegrass: at these monitoring locations Sandberg’s Bluegrass density varied from very high to low-moderate. 
The apparent disappearance of the majority of the seeded species of grasses during the second year of monitoring is problematic, and may be the result of a variety of causes.  Different technicians read the plots at different times of year between 2007 and 2008.  Seedlings may have become established the first year that later died off or went dormant because of persistent drought.  “Quadrat drift” along the paced transects used to monitor this treatment may also have played a role: density fluctuations should be evaluated cautiously.  Disappearance of most seeded species of grasses from the monitoring record the second year may not actually reflect their loss.  Data collected during the third monitoring year may help clarify these problems. 
2009 – Thickspike Wheatgrass density at CHWS – 01 exceeded the target density by nearly four times.  Thickspike Wheatgrass density at CHWS – 02 exceeded the target density by nearly five times.  Total seeded species density for CHWS – 03 approaches the target density, with Thickspike wheatgrass making the greatest contribution.  Thickspike Wheatgrass density for CHWS – 04 exceeds the target density by almost five times.  At CHWS – 05, only one specimen of Snake River Wheatgrass was recorded, other seeded species were not recorded.  At CHWS – 06, Thickspike Wheatgrass exceeded the target density.  At CHWS – 07 Basin Wildrye achieved a density of one and one-half plant per square meter during the final year: other seeded species were not recorded.  Abundant spring rains in later May and early June apparently benefited the establishment and success of this treatment with the monitoring period.  Thickspike Wheatgrass typically made the greatest contribution to seeded species density, exceeding the target density of three plants per square meter by four to five times at CHWS – 01, CHWS – 02, and CHWS – 04.  The other seeded grass species appeared to return during the final year of monitoring, suggesting that their absence during 2008 only reflected dormancy and not extirpation.  Many previously unrecorded species appeared in the native release at monitoring sites across the treatment, also reflecting the abundant later spring precipitation.  “On average,” considering the extremely high densities recorded for Thickspike Wheatgrass at many of the monitoring locations and how well established many seeded species appear to be across the treatment, the Charleston Aerial watershed Protection Seeding should be considered fully successful. 

BAR addition:
2007 – Total seeded species density exceeded the objective density of three plants per square meter at all monitoring locations.  Thickspike Wheatgrass typically made the greatest contribution to total seeded species density.  
2008 – Total seeded species density continued to exceed the objective density of three plants per square meter at CHWS – 01, CHWS – 02, and CHWS – 03, appearing to increase slightly at CHWS – 01 and CHWS – 02, and appearing to decline slightly at CHWS – 03.  Thickspike Wheatgrass continued to make the greatest contribution to total seeded species density.  
Minor density fluctuations should be evaluated cautiously: they may result from non-repeatability of individual quadrats along a paced transect.  At CHWS – 04 and CHWS – 05 total seeded species densities appeared to undergo steep declines.  Causes of opposite fluctuations in seeded densities between monitoring locations are unknown.  Downward trend in seeded species at CHWS – 04 and CHWS – 05 appears unrelated to competition from native release Sandberg’s Bluegrass: at these monitoring locations Sandberg’s Bluegrass density varied from very high to low-moderate. 
2009 – Small Burnet went unrecorded during the final monitoring year.  It’s presence in the seed mixture was not uniform, and lack of record for the presence of the species the final year may be the result of “quadrat drift” along the paced transects used to monitor this treatment.  Basin Big Sagebrush appeared to be well established at low to moderate densities at most monitoring locations by the close of the monitoring period.  Western Yarrow exceeded the objective density at CHWS – 03, but the species was “double seeded” at this location (as discussed in the analysis of the treatment above.)  At other locations Western Yarrow appeared well-established at low to moderate densities by the final year.  Basin Big Sagebrush and Western Yarrow were both recorded at low density at CHWS – 05. Basin Big Sagebrush was recorded at very low density and Western Yarrow was not recorded at CHWS – 07.  Results varied at the  numerous monitoring locations, but we may consider the addition of sagebrush and yarrow to the Charleston Aerial Watershed Protection Seeding partially successful. 
Regarding native release, reasons for the apparent precipitous decline in Sandberg’s Bluegrass density at CHWS – 03 from 2008 to 2009 are not known, but may reflect non-repeatability of individual quadrats along the paced transect.  Many previously unrecorded species were encountered at CHWS – 03 during 2009: they may have out-competed the Sandberg’s Bluegrass.  Alternately, the Prairie Junegrass and Kentucky Bluegrass identified during 2009 may have been previously misidentified as Sandberg’s Bluegrass.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The Idaho Department of Fish and Game has identified the burn area as one of the most urgent wildlife concerns in southern Idaho. The loss of a majority of the shrubs from the critical deer winter range may cause depredation problems in nearby farmlands, require initiation of a winter feeding program, or result in starvation of a portion of the population. Other wildlife needs, although not as dramatic, are also considered to be of utmost importance. The local television station, other news media, wildlife organizations, and the general public have expressed a strong interest in what will be done to restore the area.

At least 30 percent perennial vegetative cover is needed to prevent accelerated erosion, gullying and excessive loss of topsoil. Reseeding is needed to restore this cover, especially on the 5700 acres of highly erosive soils. The burn area has already contributed to several severe dust storms this summer in southern Idaho. Depending upon timing and intensity of spring runoff, sediment from the burn area could greatly compound already-severe problems in the Lower Rock Creek Watershed. Occasional heavy rainstorms, as well as spring runoff, could cause accelerated soil loss and gullying on the steep, denuded slopes.

Past fires on similar areas which have not been reseeded are now dominated by cheatgrass. Once established, cheatgrass greatly reduces the opportunity for desirable perennials to come back into an area. Due to highly combustible nature of this grass, repeated burns are common. Noxious weeds, which are a major concern in southern Idaho, are also likely to invade untreated burned areas. Reseeding of these areas promptly is the only feasible technique to establish perennial plants that will preclude site domination by annual grasses and other undesirable species.

Objectives:
To re-vegetate a fire damaged and highly disturbed native rangeland area
with essentially a native seed mixture of grasses and shrubs in order to stabilize the soils and
maintain the area for the betterment of wildlife habitat and watershed enrichment. Treatment
objectives would be met when at least one sagebrush seedling and 5 individuals of other seeded
species are established per nine m2 (0.11 and 1.1 plants/m2, respectively), and 50 percent of
native perennial grass plants are producing seed heads.
Planned_Implementation:
The majority of public lands (2,200 acres) in the burned area will be
aerially broadcast seeded with a seed mixture comprised primarily of mountain big sagebrush,
Idaho fescue, bluebunch wheatgrass, Sandberg bluegrass, Lewis flax and western yarrow. The
aerial application occurred in February 2007 by Thomas Helicopters Inc., End Product Contract.
Actual_Implementation: The treatment area was aerial broadcast seeded in February 2007 with a perennial species seed mixture
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Treatment Effectiveness: BLM monitoring crews visited the area in July 2007, establishing and
measuring 3 monitoring plots and two shrub density (shrub-hoop) transects. Crews recorded
plant species and density, vegetative cover, and canopy gaps using quadrat, line-point intercept
and gap intercept methods respectively.
Treatment Results: At this time objectives have been partially met. Density of all perennial
grasses is 40 plants /m\xb2 with seed heads on 58%. Seeded perennial grass density is 13.7; 30.5% of
these have seed heads. Only one species of the seeded forbs was observed, western yarrow; mean
density was 1.2 plants / m\xb2 with no seed heads.

2009 – The third growing season, monitoring indicate treatment objectives are being met.  Monitoring recorded the density of all perennial grasses at 11.7/m2. Seeded basin and mountain Wyoming big sagebrush was recorded at 1.1/9 m2, and seeded perennial forbs + grasses were 5.5/m2 with 10% producing seed heads. The resumption of livestock use had been authorized after the second growing season, and the low seed head production is reflective of livestock use and not plant vigor. Overall the site has very few invasive species and a good diversity of perennial grasses, forbs, and shrubs.  The site is recovering well and meeting objectives.

Planned_Implementation:
Approximately 490 acres previously characterized by generally fair
condition juniper is in need of aerial seeding, due to risk of
cheatgrass expansion. Aerial seeding is necessary because numerous
burned juniper skeletons preclude drill-seeding. Chaining would be cost
prohibitive. Aerial seeding is expected to succeed due to soil surface
roughness, numerous small crevices and the presence of soft ash/burned
duff around the burned junipers. These factors should provide an
adequate niche for the small seeds to lodge in and germinate.
Pre-burn herbaceous species included Sandberg's bluegrass, predominantly,
with bluebunch wheatgrass, Idaho fescue, western wheatgrass, Koeleria,
and Thurber&$s needlegrass present in varying amounts depending on aspect
and topographic position. Drill seeding is precluded due to the
presence of numerous juniper skeletons. The grass seed mix selected
(Sherman big bluegrass, Canbar Canby bluegrass, Covar sheep fescue,
Koeleria) are well-adapted to the site, and are expected to successfully
establish. Small seeded species such as these are often recommended for
aerial seedings and where there is likelihood that seeds will lodge in
soil crevices
Actual_Implementation:

pounds bulk seed per acre. The seed was applied to 100% snow covered ground, see the attached
map for the project location. The contractor was Reeder Flying Service of Twin Falls, ID. Pilot for the
seeding was Dick Reeder. The project was completed using a helicopter and two sling type buckets.

To date the majority of East Slide fire rehab work is completed leaving only the aerial sagebrush seeding to
be done this winter.
The project consisted of aerially seeding Wyoming big sagebrush to 800 acres within drainages and swells that burned at high severity. Seeding occurred in late fall of 2008.
The Twin Falls District Operations staff ensured that all contract specifications were met during these aerial seeding operations, that the areas planned for sagebrush seeding got done and that all work was completed in an efficient and timely manner.

Belt transects will be added to the monitoring protocol next year to determine the presence of seedlings.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The burned area was previously known to be Low Sage and Mountain big sagebrush with native bunchgrass understory, verified by the Jarbidge Vegetation Map. Sagebrush has a
minimal survival rate following intense fires. The areas of this fire that burned severely were sagebrush areas. Aerial seedlings are intended to be an effective means for establishment of sagebrush. The treatment is resource effective in that it is rehabilitating a sagebrush area towards its previous state. Arial seeding will have no damage to any resources, while improving habitat for Sage grouse and other sagebrush obligates.

Sage grouse are being considered for listing under the Endangered Species Act. The fire burned in designated sage grouse nesting, brood rearing and winter range habitat. The fire removed sagebrush cover critical for sage grouse forage during the winter and nesting habitat during the spring. There are five sage grouse leks located within 2 miles from the burn area and the majority (70%) of sage grouse nest within 3.2 miles of a lek. The area is also used by sage-grouse as brood habitat in the summer and early fall.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: The Twin Falls Management Framework Plan, completed in 1981, identifies the need to maintain or improve the area for wildlife and watershed values. The fire occurred in a yearlong antelope range and in sage grouse critical winter and yearlong ranges as well as in critical nesting and brood reading areas. Other MFP objectives include, but are not limited to, maintain existing perennial forage plants, maintain and protecting soil stability and increasing the availability of perennial forage plants.\r\n\r\nSince the perennial vegetative was lost due to fire, annuals will colonize this 2000 acre site. Without competition from perennials, Halogeton, tumble mustard and cheatgrass will establish themselves to the exclusion of more desirable perennials. Reseeding the feasible areas with perennials will achieve more effectively the objectives of reducing soil erosion, increasing available water holding of the soil and increasing the short and long term productivity.
Conditions_At_Trt_Desc: 3 inches of snow on ground

Objectives: Without treatment the burned areas are extremely susceptible to exotic annual dominance; this would jeopardize the greater sage grouse, mule deer herds and other wildlife that depend on this area year-round and especially in the winter months. Seeding occurred on sites that do not have the likelihood of naturally recovering from the fire. Areas were seeded with perennial species to reduce the dominance of Bromus tectorum. The application cost of aerial seeding is fairly high, but the risk of not seeding is the loss of species and structural diversity that will reduce the overall short and long-term value of the land. Objective: The objectives for cover will be to obtain 70% of all perennial plant cover found in the associated reference site, or, when not possible, achieve 50% of the lowest value for perennial cover associated with the appropriate ecological or range site by the end of the third year. Density objectives for aerially seeded areas will be based on having one seeded species firmly rooted per square meter by first or second growing season following seeding.
Actual_Implementation: Aerial Seeding of Sage Grouse PPH. Nevada Department of Wildlife contributed forage kochia seed. Ruby Mitigation fund contributed Mtn. Sage seed. NGO (private) contributors helped fund aircraft time for seeding.

Planned_Implementation: Aerial seeding was vital in mitigating the potential loss of Greater sage grouse habitat in the Montana, Granite, and Bilk Creek mountain ranges. T5-A2-HOL-13
Treatment: Aerially seeded A. tridentata ssp. vaseyana, L. lewisii, A. millefolium, P.

T5-A3-HOL-13
Treatment: Aerially seeded A. tridentata ssp. vaseyana, L. lewisii, A. millefolium, P.
spicata and P. tridentata.
2015: The plot meets both the ESR and livestock closure objectives for perennial cover.
The plot also meets the density of seeded species objective. P. spicata is the most
commonly occurring seeded species. B. tectorum and S. altissimum are co-dominant at the
plot. The plot has a strong bunchgrass component, with P. secunda being the most
common. On the steeper parts of the plot there are slight pedestals and terracettes.

TD-BASCO-HOL-13
Treatment: Aerially seeded A. tridentata, L. cinereus, L. lewisii, and A. millefolium.
2015: Plot does not meet the objective for density of seeded species. Perennial cover on
this plot was 12.7%. S. altissimum and B. tectorum were almost completely dominant on
this plot, with a combined coverage of over 90%. Native vegetation was rare with I.
axillaris and L. cinereus being comparatively the most common. This plot exhibited some
possible deposition from upstream due to past rain or storms. There were numerous hawks,
owls, and chukar observed near this plot, and three Greater Sage-grouse (GSG) were also
observed within 60m ESE from plot center’s UTM coordinates (refer to Table 3 for
coordinates).

T6-A1-HOL-13
Treatment: Aerially seeded A. tridentata ssp. vaseyana, A. millefolium, P. tridentata, P.
spicata and L. lewisii.
2015: The plot meets both the ESR and livestock closure objectives for perennial cover.
The plot meets the objective for density of seeded species. P. spicata is the most
successful seeded species. The plot is dominated by P. secunda; B. tectorum is subdominant.
The bunchgrass component is not as strong as expected. There is a small
amount of pedestalling on P. spicata, and the soil surface resistance to erosion is slightly
lower than expected.
2014: The plot meet both ESR and livestock closure objectives for perennial cover. The
plot does not meet the density of seeded species objective. The plot is dominated by
shallow-rooted plants, primarily P. secunda. Native forbs and shrubs are common
throughout the plot, and B. tectorum is common in areas. Deep-rooted, perennial grasses
are greatly reduced. L. lewisii is the only seeded species not present on the plot.
2013: Density of seeded species does not meet the monitoring objective. Plot meets the
ESR and livestock closure percent perennial cover objectives. From the LPI data, percent
perennial cover species include: B. sagittata, E. elmoides, Lupinus, P. secunda and P.
spicata. P. secunda co-dominates the site constituting 24% of the perennial cover, while
the plot had 18% of the annual invasive B. tectorum, which also co-dominates. One A.
tridentata ssp. vaseyana and 23 P. spicata were found along the belt transect. Seedlings
were scattered around plot, especially at the end of line 3 that crossed into a drainage. Plot
also had a rock outcrop with Symphoricarpos re-sprouting.

T6-A2-HOL-13
Treatment: Aerially seeded A. tridentata ssp. vaseyana, A. millefolium, P. tridentata, P.
spicata and L. lewisii.
2015: The plot meets the ESR objective for perennial cover, but does not meet the
livestock closure objective. The density of seeded species does not meet the monitoring
objective. This plot has a large shrub component, mostly consisting of Chrysothamnus
viscidiflorus and Symphoricarpos sp. The forb component has decreased, and B. tectorum
has increased since last monitored. The deep-rooted bunchgrasses have been heavily
grazed.
2014: The plot meets both ESR and livestock closure objectives for perennial cover. The
plot also meets the density of seeded species objective. The plot is a highly diverse, north facing
slope. Many perennial grasses, forbs, and shrubs cover the plot. Many shrubs,
especially Symphoricarpos sp., are recovering from burnt bases. All seeded species are
present except P. spicata. No invasive annual species are growing on the plot. Recent cattle
tracks and scat are present, but grazing intensity is low.
2013: Density of seeded species does not meet the monitoring objective. Plot meets the
ESR and livestock closure percent perennial cover objectives. From the LPI data, percent
perennial cover species includes 14 species. Site was very diverse and dominated by cool season,
deep-rooted, perennial grasses and re-sprouting shrubs, especially Symphoricarpos
sp. with 10% cover and combined perennial grass with 6% cover. A. millefolium seedlings
were common on site with 135 seedlings encountered within the belt transect. Two P.
spicata and one P. tridentata was also encountered along the belt transects. Very few
annual invasive plants present on plot. The very end of line 3 crossed into a different
Rangeland Ecological Site dominated by P. secunda and A. arbuscula.

T6-A1FiveMileNative-HOL-14
Treatment: Aerially seeded A. tridentata ssp. vaseyana, L. lewisii, A. millefolium, P.
spicata and P. tridentata.
2015: Plot does not meet the ESR or livestock closure objectives for perennial cover. It
does not meet the objective for density of seeded species. B. tectorum dominates the plot.
Pseudoroegneria spicata is the most common perennial plant on the plot.
2014: Density of seeded species does not meet the monitoring objective. Plot meets the
ESR percent perennial cover objective. Plot does not meet the livestock closure percent
perennial cover objective. Seeded species include fifteen P. spicata and one P. tridentata.
Deep-rooted, cool-season, perennial bunchgrasses are significantly reduced, and B.
tectorum dominates plot, reducing infiltration and compromising the area’s biotic integrity.

T6-A1LogCabin-HOL-14
Treatment: Aerially seeded A. millefolium, A. tridentata, P. spicata, L. lewisii, and P.
Tridentata
2015: The plot meets the ESR objective for perennial cover, but does not meet the
objective for livestock closure. The plot meets the objective for density of seeded species.
A. millefolium is the most successful seeded species. The plot is completely dominated by
S. altissimum, but deep-rooted bunchgrasses and some shrubs exist in the understory.
2014: The plot meets perennial cover objectives for both ESR and livestock closure. The
plot also meets the density of seeded species objective. The plot is heavily vegetated with a
high diversity of grasses, forbs and shrubs. Invasive annuals such as B. tectorum, S.
altissimum, and D. pinnata are nearly equal with native perennials. Three of the seeded
species, A. millefolium, A. tridentata, and P. spicata have been established on the site while
two species, L. lewisii and P. tridentate, are absent.

Objectives: The objectives for cover will be to obtain 70% of all perennial plant cover found in the associated reference site, or, when not possible, achieve 50% of the lowest value for perennial cover associated with the appropriate ecological or range site by the need of the third year. Density objectives for aerially seeded areas will be based on having one seeded species firmly rooted per square meter by first or second growing season following seeding.
Planned_Implementation: Aerial seeding was vital in mitigating the potential loss of Greater sage grouse habitat in the Montana, Granite, and Bilk Creek mountain ranges. Without treatment the burned areas are extremely susceptible to exotic annual dominance; this would jeopardize the Greater sage grouse, mule deer herds and other wildlife that depend on this area year-round and especially in the winter months. The areas selected are predominantly upland areas where topography is unsuitable for drill seeding due to slope and accessibility. All aerial seeding occurred in sage grouse PPH or PGH that was severely burned. Sage grouse habitat in the Bilk, Trout Creek, and Montana Mountains is widely regarded as being exceptionally productive when compared with other areas designated as sage grouse PPH. The application cost of aerial seeding is fairly high, but the risk of not seeding is the loss of species and structural diversity that will reduce the overall short and long-term value of the land.
Actual_Implementation: Original ESR-funded aerial contract was for 45,284 acres. Since contract bid was based on pounds of seed, not acres, some leftover seed from original project (avoided unburned islands) was used to increase treatment area with ESR funds. Nevada Dept. of Wildlife, Ruby Mitigation Fund, and NGO private contributors also contributed seed and aircraft time to increase accomplishments.

tridentata ssp. wyomingensis is the only other seeded species growing on the plot. Soil
stability is reduced, and water-flow patterns are present.
2013: Density of seeded species does not meet the monitoring objective. Plot meets the
ESR percent perennial cover objective. Plot does not meet the livestock closure percent
perennial cover objective. Only one seeded A. tridentata ssp. wyomingensis seedling was
observed along the belt transect. No other seeded species was observed. Deep-rooted, coolseason
perennial bunchgrass cover is less than expected but are re-sprouting well. B.
tectorum is present on plot and constitutes 9% cover. Perennial forbs constitute 7% of the

T9-A1RodeoFlat-HOL-14
Treatment: Aerially seeded with A. hymenoides, A. cristatum, A. tridentata ssp.
wyomingensis, A. canescens, B. prostrata, L. cinereus, and P. secunda.

stated objective. Perennial coverage at this plot was 24.0%, which exceeded the ESR
objective but does not meet the livestock closure objective. The high density of seeded
species was almost entirely due to a proliferation of P. secunda on the plot, and it was
impossible to determine if the counted individuals were from the 2013 seeding or natural
recruitment and regeneration. B. tectorum was still dominant on this plot (51.3%), but P.
secunda coverage was 23.3% and Amsinckia coverage was 10.7%. Litter was also very
high at this site (90.0%), especially considering this plot was monitored in mid-July while
the growing season was still ongoing. S. altissimum, D. pinnata, S. tragus, and E.
cicutarium were also present on this plot.
2014: The plot does not meet ESR or livestock closure objectives for perennial cover. The
plot meets the objective for density of seeded species. Annual species B. tectorum and
Amsinckia sp. dominate the plot. P. secunda and L. cinereus are common on the site. Soil
stability is reduced, and extensive water-flow patterns and pedestals on perennial plants
indicate that soil loss is occurring by both water and wind erosion.

of A. tridentata, L. cinereus, and A. millefolium are growing throughout the site, while the
other seeded species, L. lewisii, is absent from the plot.

transects, 63 seeded Artemisia seedlings were observed. No other seeded species was found
along the belt transects. Most of the seeded Artemisia was near the creek, and as the line

present in disturbed areas.

axillaris and L. cinereus being comparatively the most common. This plot exhibited some

observed within 60m ESE from plot center’s UTM coordinates (refer to Table 3 for
coordinates).

thick with lots of annual mustards and Iva. axillaris. Several perennial grasses are scattered
throughout the plot at moderate density. Two seeded species, L. cinereus and A.
millefolium are successfully established on the plot, while the other two species, A.
tridentata and L. lewisii, are not present on the plot.
2013: Density of seeded species meets the monitoring objective. 35 A. millefolium, 8 L.
lewisii and one L. cinereus were observed within the 1m x 1m quadrats along the transects.

disturbed areas.

2013: Density of seeded species does not meet the monitoring objective. No seeded species

but not along the belt transects. Deep-rooted, cool-season perennial bunchgrasses are resprouting
from the burn. B. tectorum is scattered throughout the plot and constitutes 5%
cover. Due to drift issues, only L. cinereus and L. lewisii made it to the riparian area. Cows
were observed within the burn before monitoring was conducted. Perennial vegetation had
been grazed by cattle

Density objectives for aerially seeded areas will be based on having one seeded species firmly rooted per square meter by first or second growing season following seeding.
Planned_Implementation: Aerial seeding was vital in mitigating the potential loss of Greater sage grouse habitat in the Montana, Granite, and Bilk Creek mountain ranges. Without treatment the burned areas are extremely susceptible to exotic annual dominance; this would jeopardize the Greater sage grouse, mule deer herds and other wildlife that depend on this area year-round and especially in the winter months. The areas selected are predominantly upland areas where topography is unsuitable for drill seeding due to slope and accessibility. All aerial seeding occurred in sage grouse PPH or PGH that was severely burned. Sage grouse habitat in the Bilk, Trout Creek, and Montana Mountains is widely regarded as being exceptionally productive when compared with other areas designated as sage grouse PPH. The application cost of aerial seeding is fairly high, but the risk of not seeding is the loss of species and structural diversity that will reduce the overall short and long-term value of the land.

Seed mixtures comprised of native shrubs and stabilizing mixes of native grasses would be

ESR Monitoring Report 2022
S3 Aerial Seeding 
Treatment(s) 
Pockets of suitable planting sites, areas where the seeded species would typically grow under normal conditions, were present across fire perimeter. Suitable sites are often difficult to delineate post-fire, covering the entire area better ensured all suitable sites were seeded. 
Contractors initially seeded 14,569 acres by helicopter on January 19, 2013; 473 acres were seeded with the grass/sagebrush mix- mix 1 (100% coverage), 6,392 acres were seeded with the forb/sagebrush mix - mix 2 (70% coverage - 375’ swath width), and 7,704 acres were seeded with the sagebrush mix - mix 3 (100% coverage). Aerial seeding density was not conducted in 2013; however, ESR personnel made numerous site visits to look for germination of seeded species during installation of vegetation recovery monitoring plots. Seven of the eleven 
Contractors re-treated 6,835 acres on February 27, 2014 (see re-treatment rationale for more information). Wyoming big sagebrush was seeded by helicopter (50% coverage – 250’ swath width, skip seeding). 

2014 Aerial Seeding Mix
Sagebrush density monitoring was not conducted in 2017. 
This objective was met in 2015 due to the reseeding in February of 2014. In August of 2015, in suitable sites, six transects of density hoop monitoring were conducted in areas that were aerially seeded with sagebrush. Locations seeded with Wyoming big sagebrush were meeting the objective with a density of 7.1 seedlings per 10m2. Low sagebrush seeding areas (Artemisia arbuscula) were not monitored. 
Large patches of sagebrush seedlings were noted at grass monitoring plots 1-2, 1-2, 2-3, 2-5, 4-1, and 5-1, and in the wilderness plot 3-1. Seedlings were 1-18” in height and appeared healthy; many were beginning to flower. Trace amounts of sagebrush were found in areas seeded with low sagebrush.

Grass density monitoring was not conducted in 2017. 
Site assessments were conducted in areas favorable for germination and establishment of perennial seeded grasses. No seedlings were observed in 2013, even in highly suitable areas where terrain would have naturally collected seed (e.g., crevices, near drainages). 
Overall, this objective was met in 2015. Areas seeded with Mix 1 in 2013 were surveyed for Sandberg bluegrass and Idaho fescue grass density in 2015. Seeded grass density ranged from 1 to 22 Sandberg bluegrass plants per 1 m2 and 0 to 8 Idaho fescue plants per 1 m2. Idaho fescue plants were noted in 5 quadrats of 9 total quadrats surveyed.

Canopy gap of aerially seeded species was not conducted in 2017.

Other Results 
In late June 2022, ESR staff qualitatively monitored four plots. 
The aspen (Populus tremuloides) stand at plot G1MKPPASP1 showed very good recovery with trees 6-8 feet tall (photo below). Snowbrush ceanothus (Ceanothus velutinus) was in poor condition due to heavy browse by elk. Due to landscape position and elevation snow sits longer at this plot. Plant phenology was a few weeks behind communities in the flat; bottlebrush squirreltail (Elymus elymoides) was just beginning to bloom on June 29th. Yarrow (Achillea millefolium) was abundant across the site. Large patches of bare soil persist but they have not filled in with either cheatgrass or noxious weeds. Though a few shrubs have resprouted, the area is functionally a grassland.

A former low sagebrush (Artemisia arbuscula) site, the plant community at plot G1MKT02 is now primarily Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda), bluebunch wheatgrass (Psuedoroegneria spicata) and bottlebrush squirreltail (photos below). Many of the bluebunch bases had dead inner cores which may have occurred due to the drought in 2021. A handful of sagebrush seedlings were found. Forb diversity included lava aster (Ionactis alpina), lupine (Lupinus sp.), willowherb (Epilobium brachycarpum), hawksbeard (Crepis sp.), pale agoseris (Agoseris glauca), hatless daisy (Erigeron aphanactis), and longleaf phlox (Phlox longifolia). Sandberg bluegrass was subdominant (10-40% abundance) across the site interspersed with small gravel.

Plot G1MKT05 falls in a small draw in Owens Pasture 1 which was representative of draws within the pasture. The plot was heavily invaded with cheatgrass and tall tumblemustard (Sisimbrium altissimum) (photos below). Bottlebrush squirreltail and yellow rabbitbrush (Chrysothamnus viscidiflorus) were present at low abundance. A few crested wheatgrass (Agropyron cristatum) plants were also noted at this plot.

G1MKNT04 was not treated as part of the Jacks ESR plan. Sandberg bluegrass and bottlebrush squirreltail have recovered well though cheatgrass fills interspaces in the gravel soil surface in 2022.

RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS 
Canopy gap objectives were not met in either Owens or Northwest allotments though most pastures were within 6% of the objective. Invasive non-native annuals have increased significantly at some plots, particularly in pasture 12 of the Northwest allotment. Perennial grasses have increased in size since 2013, were producing seed heads and plants were in good vigor. Overall, site assessments and photos indicate that perennial grasses have recovered in both treated and natural recovery areas. Grazing was resumed in Owens Allotment in June 2015 (see Part 12: Additional Information). Monitoring ten years post-fire shows very good grass recovery across the burned area. Though there are some patches of cheatgrass present, no large expanses occur in the fire perimeter. 
The aerial sagebrush seeding objective was met in 2015 due to the reseeding in February of 2014. Moisture in February and March of 2014 were above average as was late summer and fall moisture; this likely helped with the establishment and growth of the seeded sagebrush. Sagebrush seedlings may have been missed or not yet germinated and emerged during monitoring in 2014 but were picked up during monitoring of 2015. Few sagebrush seedlings were found during ten-year monitoring in 2022. Much of the Jacks fire is now functionally a grassland. 
Canada thistle is common throughout the Big Jacks Creek riparian corridor and due its extent, chemical treatment will not be implemented. These sites will be targeted for biological control releases in the future. A population of Scotch thistle detected at the reservoir in 2014 was treated in 2015. It is expected this treatment will be effective but both sites will require continued monitoring to prevent re-establishment. Although the most likely areas for invasion have been inventoried, continued monitoring of treatment sites and the burned area is recommended. Continued monitoring should focus on travel corridors and highly disturbed sites

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
S-3 Aerial seeding- This stabilization aerial seeding on the upper parts of the Kelly Ck project returned an average of 0.5 seeded species per square meter, all of which was forage kochia. This did not meet our initial objective of 3 plants per square meter, which we now believe to be unrealistic. Our experience, particularly with forage kochia, has demonstrated to us that we often will not get a ‘good signal’ on germination and establishment until the 2nd or 3rd. year following the treatment.  We did observe a good distribution of seeded plants in the areas we traveled through, including our sites, to have good confidence in coverage and eventual establishment. These plants will reduce herbivory impacts on recovering grasses, plants responsible for the majority of soil surface stability.
2010 Summary results:
Aerial Stabilization Results:
Density: Seeded species in this treatment area were present yet broadly spaced
(35-50 meters) with KOPR80 being the dominant seeded species and MESA occurring in
trace amounts.
SA-1 was established in 2009 with density results consisting exclusively of KOPR80.
(Note; Livestock were found congregating at the end of the transect during monitoring.) All
seeded species had been grazed, but seemed to have some seedling recruitment. 2010 
monitoring showed a decrease in density and approximately 85% of the recorded KOPR80
showed signs of herbivory.
SA-2 was established in 2010, therefore, no previous data exists for trend analysis.
Monitoring had a similar outcome as SA-1 with KOPR80 as the only seeded species
recorded--also heavily grazed--and livestock were observed throughout the area during
monitoring. Both densities were below objectives, however, when assessing the success of
these sites it is important to consider that both fall within a lower precipitation zone (8-
10") than the Aerial Rehabilitation sites in addition to the challenges posed to seedling
establishment by unauthorized grazing.
Foliar Cover: Values exceeded objectives at both sites. SA-1 showed good recovery
of native grasses and forbs during 2009 monitoring with 3.3% of the total foliar cover
consisting of KOPR80. 2010 monitoring showed some diversity loss and KOPR80 was not
recorded during line point intercept, however, foliar cover objectives were still surpassed.
During 2010 SA-2 monitoring it was noted that there was very good native grass
recovery, which is also reflected in the data sheets. The site had also been grazed and
seemed to have a more dominant cheatgrass understory than SA-1. KOPR80 was recorded
during line point intercept as . 7% of the foliar cover.
Although the average density is below objective, the foliar cover objectives were
exceeded. A high degree of natural recovery and seeded species establishment have
stabilized the soils and prevented erosion, therefore this treatment was moderately
successful. Continued monitoring by the interdisciplinary team is suggested in order to
observe any changes in annual/perennial cover and conduct Rangeland Health
Assessments in five year intervals from the ESR closeout date of this fire.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Soil/Water Stabilization
Dominant Rangeland Ecological Sites within the burned area are: Claypan 12-16 PZ, 025XY017NV (approx. 70%), a soil type subject to flashy overland flow, funneling water energy and flows onto the second major soil type (30%), Loamy 8-10 024XY005, causing moderate sheet and rilling erosion on lower slopes , negatively affecting drainages that support Lahontan Cutthroat Trout, a threatened species.
Designated Critical Habitat for Federal/State Listed, Proposed, or Candidate Species
This fire burned through a large portion of winter, summer and nesting sage grouse habitat. Also active leks are within a third of a mile away. The rest of the burned area’s shrub and bunchgrass community was recovering from the Humboldt Fire of 1996 and the Chimney Fire of 1997. 
The Kelly Creek fire burned a large portion of the Tuscarora Sage grouse population management unit (PMU). This and a related fire, Red Hills, burned the same week, impacting more habitat in this same PMU. Cumulative effects of last year’s Winters Fire along with this year’s fires in this area will severely impact the sage grouse populations. This sage grouse population management unit has been developed to protect, restore, improve and manage habitat for sage grouse, which is a BLM sensitive species. This fire also impacted watershed areas of fisheries in First Creek and the S. Fork of the Little Humboldt River, Designated Critical habitat for Lahontan Cutthroat Trout (LCT), a listed, threatened species.
Invasive Plants
The burned area consisted primarily of recovering Wyoming sage brush/Bunchgrass community (70%) and intact Wyoming sage brush/Bunchgrass Community (30%). These community types have become increasingly more vulnerable to burning followed by conversion to invasive annuals and noxious weeds.  Non-native invasive annual grasses, mostly cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum), are present in the vicinity of the burned area, and were present within the burned area pre-fire.  It is highly likely that seeds of this species remain viable within the seedbank in the burned area post-fire. Hoary cress (Cardaria draba), Tall Whitetop (Lepidium latifolium), Scotch thistle (Onopordum acanthium L.) and Tamarisk (Tamarix L.) are located along roads that lead into the burned area and now pose a threat to increase substantially within the burned area.

Actual_Implementation: Stabilize soils and limit erosion on upper elevation steep slopes within the burn\r\narea to reduce sedimentation into the S. Fork of the Little Humboldt River and to re-establish habitat for\r\nBLM listed sensitive species (Sage Grouse).
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
This rehabilitation aerial seeding on the upper parts of the Kelly Ck project returned an average
of 0.01 seeded species per square meter, all of which was forage kochia. This did not meet our
initial objective of 3 plants per square meter, which we now believe to be unrealistic. Our
experience, particularly with forage kochia, has demonstrated to us that we often will not get a
‘good signal’ on germination and establishment until the 2nd or 3rd. year following the treatment.
This is probably true of small burnet as well. We did observe a good distribution of seeded plants
(both forage kochia and small burnet) in the areas we traveled through, including our sites, to
have good confidence in coverage and eventual establishment. These plants will reduce
herbivory impacts on recovering grasses, plants responsible for the majority of soil surface
stability, while increasing forage for both wildlife and livestock.
2010 Summary results:
Aerial Rehabilitation Results:
Density: Overall, the treatment area has good establishment and recruitment of
seeded species. KOPR80 seems to be the most prevalent and consistently spread with
ARTRW8 establishing sparsely but with even distribution.
RA-Al density monitoring during 2008 showed trace amounts of KOPR80 within the
transect, with no other seeded species present. Second year monitoring revealed an
increase in KOPR80 density as well as the establishment of SAMI, while ARTRW8 was
present along, but not within, the transect. By 2010, KOPR80 density had increased from
2009 totals, and ARTRW8 had established within the transect signaling progress towards
the re-establishment of a Wyoming sagebrush community. Seeded species success was
high as density objectives were exceeded at this site.
RA-A2 was not established until 2010, so baseline data is not available for
comparison or trend analysis, however, KOPR80 was present within the transect and
ARTRW8 seedlings were observed nearby during 2010 monitoring. This transect is located
within a few stands of unburned sagebrush, so natural and seeded ARTRW8 recruitment is
likely to occur.
Foliar Cover: All foliar objectives were exceeded and a high degree of natural
recovery was evident in Aerial Rehabilitation sites; all perennial species recorded are
congruent with the major plant species associated with this ecological site (R025XY017NV)
while annuals provided a small percentage of the total cover.
The average density value for both sites is just shy of meeting objectives. Seeded
species have established well throughout this treatment area within a short time which has
mitigated soil erosion and sedimentation transportation to nearby -streams. Moreover
seeded species were recorded along transects during line point intercept studies
suggesting that they are now components of the vegetation structure providing forage to
support the wildlife in the area. The combination of density and foliar cover values led us
to rank this treatment as moderately successful

Objectives: The objectives for cover will be to obtain 70% of all perennial plant cover found in the associated reference site, or, when not possible, achieve 50% of the lowest value for perennial cover associated with the appropriate ecological or range site by the end of the third year. Density objectives for aerially seeded areas will be based on having one seeded species firmly rooted per square meter by first or second growing season following seeding.
Planned_Implementation:
This project proposes to aerially seed approximately 13,284 acres of PPH or PGH with seeds based on availability, adaptation, and probability of success consistent with the National Technical Team 2011 Sage-Grouse Conservation Measures; the seed mix would
include yarrow, perennial flax, mountain big sagebrush, Wyoming big sagebrush, and antelope bitterbrush. Other site-adapted native plant species will be included in addition to, or as an alternative to the identified species, depending on seed cost and/or availability. This seeding would occur between December 2012 and March 2013.
This project also proposes to aerially seed Wyoming big sagebrush over the "cheatgrass die-off' drill seeding project area. Other site-adapted native plant species may be utilized, depending on availability and cost. Approximately 2539 acres will be seeded,
and this seeding would occur between December 2012 and March 2013.
Actual_Implementation: Aerially seeded, by a contractor, 11,284 acres of Sage Grouse Preliminary Priority Habitat and/or Preliminary General Habitat with mountain sagebrush, western yarrow and Sandberg\u2019s bluegrass. The main purpose of this treatment was to stabilize wildlife habitat, with an emphasis on Sage Grouse crucial winter habitat.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
T4-A2-SalientPeak-LOCY-14
Treatment: aerially seeded with A. tridentata ssp. vaseyana, P. secunda, and A.
millefolium
2015: The plot does not meet the perennial cover objectives for ESR or livestock closure.
The plot meets the objective for density of seeded species. The plot has a diverse
population of deep-rooted, perennial bunchgrasses (Figure 13). Invasive plants are
scattered throughout the plot. There is some evidence of grazing, and many plants are
not producing seeds. Soil stability is reduced, and there is more bare ground than
expected. Areas of soil deposition are apparent on the plot.

T4-A2-LOCY-13
Treatment: aerially seeded with A. tridentata ssp. vaseyana, P. secunda, and A.
millefolium
2015: The plot meets the ESR objective for perennial cover. It does not meet the
livestock closure objective. The plot meets the objective for density of seeded species.
The flora is relatively diverse in this plot. B. tectorum is common to codominant and
occupies much of the understory. Some soil degradation has occurred, as shown by

Objectives: The seeding will help increase ground cover rapidly and help to reduce the potential for erosion and establishment of invasive plant species. Species and method selected have proven to be successful in the area. The goal of the treatment is to establish protective ground cover of perennial vegetation to protect the exposed soils from wind and water erosion, and to prevent the area from becoming dominated by annual grasses. Failure to complete seeding operations will leave the burn area open to erosion and proliferation of invasive plants, decreasing the ability of the site to provide suitable habitat for wildlife in the future.
Planned_Implementation:
Forage Kochia has been removed from this plan and seed table. 
Approximately 2,000 acres within the Olympus Fire will be aerially seeded with forage kochia (Bassia prostrata) and Ladak alfalfa (Medicago sativa). This seeding will help stabilize soils, reduce the potential for wind/water erosion on the site, and decrease opportunities for medusahead spread and established. Seeding will be done utilizing fixed wing aircraft or
helicopter. Seeding will occur in the winter of 2013-2014, which is the time Burns District along with ODFW and private landowners have been most successful for these seeded species. In the last four years these species have been used in rehabilitation of prescribed fires, wild fires, and crested seeding maintenance with a success rate greater than 75%.
Successful projects include Miller Homestead ESR aerial seeding along Hwy 205 (January 2013), Five Creeks aerial seeding rehab of drier sights (December 2011), Crow's Nest (January 2010) and Hamilton (January 2011) drill seeding with tubes polled for crested seeding maintenance in both establish crested and cheatgrass monocultures, and ODFW Tom Segal aerial seeding in burned medusahead monocultures at Jordan Valley (2011). Forage Kochia is a desirable non-native forb that has been shown to suppress invasive annual grass species, coexist with sage-steppe plant communities and stabilize disturbed
soils (Monaco et al. 2003; Newhall et al. 2004; Harrison et al. 2000; Clements et al. 1997). Past experience with the use of forage kochia on the Burns District has shown a high probability of success at using this species in fire and invasive annual grass restoration projects. Its drought tolerance, combined with extensive root systems and good seedling vigor, make this species ideal for reclamation in areas receiving 9 to 12 inches annual precipitation. Ladak alfalfa is a desirable non-native forb used for improved erosion control, forage, nutrient cycle, and cover. This forb adds diversity to the seed mix and performs
well in low precipitation zones. Ladak alfalfa and forage kochia are both considered excellent food sources for wildlife and livestock.
Actual_Implementation: Ladak Alfalfa was aerial seeded last winter however it appears that it failed with the below average precipitation in conjunction with Medusahead Rye competition.

Objectives:
The primary objective is to aerially seed burned areas at greatest risk for damage from fire effects.  Establish one seeded plant per square meter rooted firmly in soil with consideration for site selection factors of soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and potential for seedling establishment. 
 Establish one seeded plant per square meter rooted firmly in soil with consideration for site selection factors of soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and potential for seedling establishment.  Provide cover and forage for wildlife and BLM Special Status Species/migratory birds, including crucial winter habitat for mule deer, and sage grouse habitat.  

The aerial seeding will provide soil stabilization, which will reduce runoff and associated sediment loading to intermittent and ephemeral drainages; reduce the potential for invasion nonnative invasive plant species, such as cheatgrass, and noxious weeds; and provide cover and forage for area wildlife populations.  Specifically, this seeding will provide forage for pronghorn antelope and mule deer.  Other sagebrush dependent species such as sage grouse will also benefit.   Migratory birds that utilize shrubs for nesting will also benefit.  Seeding with shrub and grasses will provide deep rooted perennial plants to establish, which will help provide soil stabilization, trap snow and reduce evaporation of the moisture from the soils due to wind.  Shrub establishment will also help the establishment of natural revegetation by capturing snow and providing moisture to grasses and forbs.  The shrubs will also provide sheltered areas from the wind, which will reduce some wind erosion on the site.  All of these functions enhance the herbaceous plant community which protects the soil from potential increased soil erosion that is likely following a fire and reduces the opportunities for increases in invasive nonnative plant or noxious weed species.  Establishment of vegetation helps to stabilize watersheds and upland soils to prevent further degradation to affected resources on lands within the fire perimeter or downstream drainages that may result from short duration, high intensity precipitation events.

The seed will be applied when weather conditions are favorable to allow for coverage by snow or adequate moisture, and thus will be applied in late fall or early winter.

Actual_Implementation:
Native grass seeds were applied concurrently with the Snow Canyon Aerial Wildlife Seeding.  
This treatment was implemented during January via helicopter through an aircraft rental agreement.  AgNav maps of the aerial seeding were completed for the project file.  Aerial seeding was monitored to ensure seed was dispersed over the targeted area at the specified rate.  A project inspector ensured treatment met contract specifications. 

Additional seed: A mix of forb and shrub seeds was applied concurrently with the Snow Canyon Aerial Range Seeding. .  Because the seed was applied concurrently with the Snow Canyon Aerial Range Seeding, only seed costs are reflected here.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

The Snow Canyon Aerial Range Seeding was monitored at the same plot established to monitor the Snow Canyon Aerial Wildlife (low elevation) Seeding. 

Monitoring Results:
2007 – Of seeded grass species, only Basin Wildrye was recorded, and at low density. 
2008 – No seeded grass species were recorded.   This should be cautiously assessed, because it may result from “quadrat drift,” or non-repeatability of quadrats along a paced transect.  
2009 – Of seeded grass species, only Basin Wildrye was recorded, and at a low density just slightly higher than that recorded during 2007.  Seeded species density results during 2008 appear to have been anomalous, probably the result of quadrat drift.   Seeded Basin Wildrye is well established at low density.  Reasons for apparent lack of success of other species of grass seeded during this treatment are unknown.  Based upon Basin Wildrye alone we may consider this treatment partially successful.  

Additional seed:
Monitoring Results:
2007 – Antelope Bitterbrush was also seeded with a hand-planting method at the monitoring location. Since Antelope Bitterbrush was “double-seeded” at this monitoring location, precise determination of success by treatment is not possible.  Two Antelope Bitterbrush seedlings were recorded.  Recorded Antelope Bitterbrush probably germinated from the hand-plant treatment, not the aerial application.  Mountain Big Sagebrush was not recorded. 
2008 – One seedling of Antelope Bitterbrush and one seedling of Mountain Big Sagebrush were recorded, representing very low densities for both species.  Western Yarrow was not recorded.  
2009 – Total seeded species were recorded at a moderate density exceeding one-half plant per square meter.  Western Yarrow made the greatest contribution, and appears to be well established at a moderate density near one-half plant per square meter.  One seedling of Antelope Bitterbrush and two seedlings of Mountain Big Sagebrush were recorded, representing very low densities for both species.  On high elevation aerial wildlife seedings implemented across the District, Mountain Big Sagebrush has proven difficult to establish, so any establishment at all is encouraging for this species.  The Snow Canyon Aerial Wildlife Seeding is partially successful.

Actual_Implementation: Aerial Seeded 5,940 acres with Wyoming big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata ssp. wyomingensis).
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: Drought conditions after initial seeding treatment likely contributed to poor response of vegetation. Annual invasive species continue to dominate both plots along with a high cover of P. secunda. After three years of monitoring, neither site met density objectives, and only one of the two sites met the perennial cover objective. Extremely low densities of L. cinereus and A. millefolium were established from seeding treatments, while A. tridentata establishment failed at both plots. Both density of seeded species and perennial cover remained the same for both sites from 2013 to 2014, indicating that the areas may have reached a stable state dominated by shallow-rooted grasses with invasive annual forbs common throughout. Soil loss by wind and water erosion is evident, but not significantly increasing, which suggests that the current vegetation cover may be capable of preventing further soil loss.

Objectives:
The fire killed the shrub component within the burn perimeter.   The goal of reseeding the treatment areas with shrub species is to help provide cover and forage for wildlife; reduce water erosion hazards by stabilizing soils; increase the rate at which native riparian vegetation is restored; maintain a healthy, productive, and diverse plant community; and minimize the establishment of exotic annual plants.  

Emphasis of these rehabilitation seedings have been placed on mule deer, antelope, and sage grouse.  Application of sagebrush seed will target areas that had the existing vegetation community that is being seeded.  

The primary objective of the treatment is to seed areas of the burn that are at high risk for significant erosion and non-native species invasion.
Planned_Implementation: \u2022\tMule Deer Winter Range Seeding \u2013 Aerially seed approximately 11,550 acres with a mix which consists of Mountain big sagebrush, Basin big sagebrush, and Western yarrow.  Treatment emphasis was placed on the most critical areas for mule deer winter range using ecological sites based on vegetation mortality, soil types, precondition vegetation, and consultation with the Nevada Department of Wildlife.
Actual_Implementation: A Mule Deer Winter Range mix of Mountain and Basin big sagebrush and Western Yarrow was applied. \r\nThis treatment was done in December with a helicopter through and aircraft rental agreement. AgNav maps of the aerial seeding were completed for the project file. Aerial seeding was monitored to ensure that seed was being dispersed in the proper area and at the specified rate. A project inspector was present throughout the process to ensure the treatment met contract specifications.

Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

The following invasive/ potentially invasive species were observed within the transect: BRTE, SIAL, LEPE and DEPI
