Objectives:
To establish three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment; to provide cover and forage for wildlife.

Overall Seeding Application
Broadcast seed on approximately 12,699 acres with the two different seed mixtures shown below.  Treatments would be completed aerially such as use of a helicopter with seed broadcast bucket.  Seeding  grasses and forbs within drainages would allow for watershed protection and will reduce erosion potential.  The seeding of big sagebrush and Western yarrow would help provide cover and forage for approximately 200 wildlife species that inhabit sagebrush habitats including sage grouse and mule deer (both Resource Management Plan-featured species), migratory birds and Special Status Species.  It would also provide vegetation needed for ecological site dynamics.
Planned_Implementation:
Aerially seed approximately 14,500 acres with Wyoming big sagebrush and Western yarrow. 


Wyoming Big Sagebrush/Western Yarrow Mix Portion of  Overall Seeding Application
Broadcast seed on every third 60-foot swath which would equal approximately 12,219 acres within 37,026 acres. Wyoming big sagebrush and Western yarrow would be applied at 0.25 pounds pure live seed (PLS) per acre an 0.15 pounds PLS per acre, respectively.  This consideration includes a “no seeding” buffer of 400 feet on main roads and two-tracks for potential future fuel break planning, private lands and the estimated 10% unburned areas within the perimeter.
Actual_Implementation: The Aerial Wildlife seed mixture included Basin Wildrye, Western Yarrow, and Wyoming Big Sagebrush.  Basin Wildrye was only added to two of the bags used in this treatment.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
The aerial wildlife seeding on the Wilson burn was monitored at three sites, one in each allotment affected by the fire. 
Monitoring Results: 
2006 – Success of the Wilson aerial wildlife seeding varied from monitoring plot to monitoring plot.  The first year of monitoring indicated generally low rates of germination and establishment for Western Yarrow and Wyoming Big Sagebrush.  Treatment success was higher in the Petan-Owyhee Unit range allotment: there the soil surface seemed to have undergone less erosion and appeared to offer a better seedbed than on the YP and Owyhee grazing allotments.  In the YP and Owyhee allotments, seeded species establishment was low after first year of growth.  No seeded species were observed outside quadrats or off transect in the YP Allotment, though an effort was made to locate the transect within the seeding aircraft’s flight path. On both the YP grazing allotment and Owyhee grazing allotment monitoring sites, there appeared to be considerable surface erosion, with pedestaling of Sandberg’s Bluegrass that survived the fire.  The exposed soil surface between pedestaled grass crowns was smooth and seemed relatively impervious to penetration of broadcast seed under normal circumstances.  Except for surface cracking initiated by high clay content, favorable seedbed appeared scarce.  There is little or no Cheatgrass on the monitoring sites, and cheatgrass establishment on uplands across the Wilson burn is generally low.  Failure of Cheatgrass to establish on burn uplands may result from the same unfavorable soil surface factors that appear to have retarded establishment of aerially seeded species. 
2007 – Changes in recorded densities of seeded species appear insignificant, and result from inability to replicate quadrat placement precisely along paced transects from year to year.  Native release species remain at densities comparable to those recorded during 2006. 
2008 – Success of the Aerial Wildlife Seeding across the wide areas treated on the Wilson Burn was variable but generally poor and appeared to respond to conditions such as ground surface conditions relative to seedbed favorability, localized drought, and competition from preexisting vegetation.  Germination and establishment rates for all seeded species were low, especially in the YP and Owyhee grazing allotments.  Fluctuations were insignificant and densities remained at very low levels throughout the monitoring period.  On the Petan-Owyhee Unit grazing allotment germination and establishment rates for aerially seeded species were slightly higher, and appeared to decline over the monitoring period. 
The monitoring plot (WIWI-01) was established as a paced transect to monitor the Aerial Wildlife Seeding applied at this location. The monitoring plot is located on a flat tableland (Peterson Table), a stable geomorphic surface subject to very little erosion or deposition.  The soil surface appears to have lost about one-half inch of topsoil, leaving a polished fine-textured surface high in clay and low in organic matter in plant interspaces.  The site appears to be high- to mid-seral and Sandberg’s Bluegrass-dominated, but range condition may be good at this site.  Bluebunch Wheatgrass contributes substantially to the visual aspect here, and density numbers for the species suggest this species remains a major component of the vegetation at this location.  Idaho Fescue and Letterman’s Needlegrass are also present.  
AERIAL WILDLIFE SEEDING
The Aerial Wildlife seed mixture included Basin Wildrye, Western Yarrow, and Wyoming Big Sagebrush.  Basin Wildrye was only added to two of the bags used in this treatment.   Such limited application might not be recorded at randomly selected study plots.  The exact area of the aerial broadcast of the bags containing Basin Wildrye was unknown when plots were established.  Basin Wildrye was neither recorded nor observed at this location, either as seeded or native release plants.  
Western Yarrow appears to have germinated at very low density, and then was not recorded during the second two years of monitoring.  Fluctuations may result from lack of repeatability of individual quadrats along a paced transect, so conclusions regarding success or failure of any given seeded species based upon fluctuating density numbers may be confounded by sampling error resulting from non-repeatability of individual quadrats along a paced transect.  Taking this into account, if we are confident in numbers suggesting decrease of Western Yarrow here, it is likely that localized persistent drought interfered with establishment of Western Yarrow Seedlings subsequent to germination. 
Wyoming Big Sagebrush was recorded at very low density during the second year of monitoring only.  Wyoming Big Sagebrush was the only species aerially seeded for wildlife on the Wilson burn.  Over large areas affected by the Wilson burn the shrub component of the potential natural community (PNC) on bench lands and at middle elevations is Basin Big Sagebrush.  For unknown reasons across these areas peripheral to the Owyhee Desert, Basin Big Sagebrush appears to have filled the niche normally occupied by Wyoming Big Sagebrush. Wyoming Big Sagebrush seems to be more difficult to establish than Basin Big Sagebrush.  It may be more susceptible to drought stress during the seedling stage than Basin Big Sagebrush.  Wyoming Big Sagebrush appears to have a narrower ecological tolerance than Basin Big Sagebrush.  
The Aerial Wildlife Seeding was only marginally successful at this location based upon very low density of Western Yarrow appearing to decrease by the end of the three-year monitoring period, and very low density of Wyoming Big Sagebrush.  Western Yarrow was observed off transect at very low densities.  Ultimate establishment of seeded Wyoming Big Sagebrush on this site is not assured, and seems unlikely since the local PNC includes Basin Big Sagebrush instead.  Competition from dense, well-established Sandberg’s Bluegrass and soil surface factors contributing to an unfavorable seedbed may have also limited success of the aerially broadcast seeding at this location. 
The monitoring plot (WIWI-02) was established as a paced transect to monitor the Aerial Wildlife Seeding applied at this location.  The monitoring plot is located on a flat tableland, a stable geomorphic surface subject to little erosion or deposition.  Little surface soil loss appears to have occurred at this location.  The transect runs north within the flight path of the aircraft that was used for the aerial broadcast, nearly parallel to the access road.  Vegetation appears to be seral and degraded, and is dominated by Sandberg’s Bluegrass and Hood’s Phlox.  Range condition may have been at the low end of fair prior to the burn: very few high-quality range forage grasses were observed at this location.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The 2005 Wilson Fire Complex burned approximately 53,228 acres including 41,986 acres of BLM-administered public lands, 10,864 acres of private lands and 267 acres on the Duck Valley Indian Reservation.  Burn severity was generally light with areas throughout where burn severity was moderate.  Regardless, with the exception of the estimated 10% unburned areas (“islands”) primarily on the mid and south central portion, there was the complete loss of shrubs in blocks of land over several thousand acres within the burn perimeter.  This is a major concern since there are minimal numbers of unburned areas within these blocks to serve as future big sagebrush seed sources.

The purpose of the proposed action described in the emergency stabilization and rehabilitation plan and this EA is to protect the burned area from livestock grazing, seed the burned area to stabilize the soils and prevent the establishment of annual and invasive nonnative plant species, allow the undamaged plant species time to re-establish, and treat the invasive nonnative plant species, namely Scotch thistle, Canada thistle, musk thistle and hoary cress, to prevent spreading.  The need for the proposed action is to&* stabilize and prevent unacceptable degradation to natural and cultural resources&* minimize threats to life or property resulting from the effects of the fire&* construct physical improvements necessary to prevent degradation of land or resources and to prescribe cost effective post-fire stabilization measures necessary to protect human life, property, and critical cultural and natural resources.

The proposed seeding would help stabilize the watershed to prevent further degradation to affected resources on lands within the fire perimeter or downstream drainages that may result from high intensity precipitation events&* reduce the potential for invasive nonnative weeds and competitive annual plant species&* help provide forage, cover, and habitat for wildlife, including but not limited to, BLM designated special status species, migratory birds, mule deer, pronghorn antelope, and sage grouse.

Objectives: The primary objective of the treatment is to aerially seed areas of the fire that are critical to wildlife, or most at risk for long-term irreversible damage due to the effects of the fire. Sagebrush and yarrow were seeded to add vegetation structure and species richness to the treatment areas.\r\nEstablish one seeded plant per square meter rooted firmly in soil with consideration for site selection factors of soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and potential for seedling establishment.  Provide cover and forage for wildlife and BLM Special Status Species/migratory birds, including crucial winter habitat for mule deer, and sage grouse habitat.
Planned_Implementation: Aerially seed approximately 3,082 acres with a mixture of Western Yarrow and Mountain Big Sagebrush.
Actual_Implementation: The Aerial Wildlife (high elevation) Seeding was completed during December via helicopter through a rental agreement.  The ground crew consisted of BLM helitack and a project inspector.  AG Nav maps of the aerial seeding were completed for the project file.  Aerial seeding was monitored to ensure seed was dispersed over the target area at the specified rate.  A project inspector ensured treatment met contract specifications.\r\n\r\n2007 monitoring summary states treatment implemented in January.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

The Aerial Wildlife (High Elevation) Seeding was monitored at one location on a convex upland south of Dry Creek drainage. 
Monitoring Results: 
2007 – Western Yarrow was recorded at very low density.  Mountain Big sagebrush was not recorded.  The monitoring location supported moderate density of Mulesear after the first year.  This location appears to be an area that supported Arrowleaf Balsamroot in the potential natural community.  The balsamroot has been largely replaced by Mulesear, perhaps subsequent to grazing disturbance.  The Mulesear density is moderate; but high canopy cover and competition from Mulesear may have suppressed seeded species germination and establishment. NA
2008 – Western Yarrow density increased from very low, to low density.  Mountain Big Sagebrush was recorded at very low density (one plant was recorded.)  The Mulesear that dominates the monitoring location increased in density slightly. 
2009 – Western Yarrow was recorded at moderate density.  Mountain Big Sagebrush was not recorded.  Mulesear appeared to decline in density.  Fluctuations should be assessed cautiously because individual quadrat frames along a paced transect (beyond the first photographed frame) are not perfectly repeatable.  Minor fluctuations in density may result from “quadrat drift.”  Because both seeded species were recorded during the monitoring period, and Western Yarrow consistently increased and appears to be well-established at low-to-moderate density, this seeding may be considered partially successful at the monitoring location.

Objectives: The primary objective is to aerially seed burned areas critical to wildlife, or at greatest risk for irreversible damage because of fire effects.  \r\nEstablish one seeded plant per square meter rooted firmly in soil with consideration for site selection factors of soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and potential for seedling establishment.  Provide cover and forage for wildlife and BLM Special Status Species/migratory birds, including crucial winter habitat for mule deer, and sage grouse habitat.
Planned_Implementation: Aerially seed approximately 7,067 acres with a mixture of Western Yarrow and Basin Big Sagebrush.
Actual_Implementation:
Sagebrush and yarrow were seeded to add vegetation structure and species richness to treated areas.  

The Aerial Wildlife (Mid-elevation) Seeding was completed during December by helicopter through an aircraft rental agreement.  The ground crew consisted of BLM helitack and a project inspector.  AG Nav maps of the aerial seeding were completed for the project file.  Aerial seeding was monitored to ensure seed was dispersed over the target area at the specified rate.  The project inspector ensured treatment met contract specifications.

2007 monitoring summary states this treatment was implemented in January.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

The Aerial Wildlife (Mid-elevation) Seeding was monitored at four separate locations.  One location along a tributary of Little Rock Creek (WNWC – 03) was specifically established to monitor this treatment.  The other locations (WNWC – 02, WNWP – 01, WNWP – 02) were established to monitor aerial watershed protection seedings but are overlapped by the Aerial Wildlife (Mid-elevation) Seeding. 
Monitoring Results: 
2007 – Western Yarrow and Basin Big Sagebrush were “double-seeded” at WNWC – 02 where the Aerial Watershed Protection (Lahontan Cutthroat Trout) Seeding overlapped the Aerial Wildlife (Mid-elevation) Seeding, and at WNWP – 01 and WNWP – 03 where the Aerial Watershed Protection (Milligan/Chimney Creeks) Seeding overlapped the Aerial Wildlife (Mid-elevation) Seeding.  At locations where double-seeding occurred, seedlings contributed by either treatment cannot be separated: it is impossible to make a precise determination concerning which treatment was successful.  Since no rational separation of seedlings contributed by either treatment at the double-seeded locations can be made, total densities of the double seeded species are presented in the summaries for both treatments.  Caution should be applied when interpreting these density numbers with regard to either treatment: ultimately, we cannot know which treatment contributed any given seedling. 
2008 – Results varied at the five monitoring locations.  Total seeded species were recorded at low moderate density at WNWC – 02, at moderate density at WNWC – 03, and at very low density at WNWP – 03. Seeded species were not recorded at WNWP – 01 and WNWP – 02. 
2009 – Results continued to vary at the five monitoring locations, and fluctuated both up and down from 2008.  Generally, Western Yarrow appeared to be well-established at low density by the final year of the monitoring period.  At WNWC – 03, total seeded species exceeded the target density of one seeded plant per square meter, with Western Yarrow making the greatest contribution at nearly one plant per square meter.  Wyoming Big Sagebrush was less successful.  The seeding was only fully successful at WNWC – 03.  At most sites the seeding was partially successful.  At WNWP – 01 no seeded species were observed during the monitoring period.  Ocular reconnaissance across widely separated seeded areas supports confidence in a conclusion of partially successful.  Generally, Basin Big Sagebrush was less successful than Western Yarrow.  Causes of the general lack of success of Basin Big Sagebrush in this seeding are unknown, because it usually establishes readily.

Objectives: Reseeding with shrubs will help provide cover and forage for wildlife, reduce water and wind erosion, maintain a healthy, productive, diverse plant community, and minimize establishment of exotic annual plants.  Application of sagebrush seed will target areas that formerly supported sagebrush, to increase success of the seeding by ensuring seeded species are applied in areas suitable for establishment.  \r\nEstablish three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in soil with consideration for site selection factors of soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and potential for seedling establishment.  Establish sagebrush stands within the burned area as future seed sources to repopulate hundreds of square miles.  Provide cover and forage for wildlife and BLM Special Status Species/migratory birds, including crucial winter habitat for mule deer, and sage grouse habitat.
Planned_Implementation: Aerially seed approximately 37,120 acres with Wyoming Big Sagebrush (\u201cDesert Unit mixture\u201d).
Actual_Implementation: The Aerial Wildlife (Desert Unit) Seeding was completed in December via helicopter through an aircraft rental agreement.  The ground crew consisted of BLM helitack and a project inspector. AG Nav maps of the aerial seeding were completed for the project file.  Aerial seeding was monitored to ensure seed was dispersed over the target area at the specified rate.  The project inspector ensured treatment met contract specifications.\r\n\r\n2007 monitoring report states treatment completed in December and January.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

The Aerial Wildlife (Desert Unit) Seeding was monitored at eleven separate locations.  Three monitoring plots were established to monitor this treatment with paced density transects (WNWI – 03, WNWI – 04, and WNWC – 01.)  The additional eight plots were established to monitor disjunct drill seedings (overlapped by the Desert Unit seeding) with permanent modified Freqdens transects (WNND – 01, WNND – 03, WNND – 04, WNND – 05, WNND – 06, WNND – 07, WNND – 09, WNND – 10.) 
Monitoring Results:
2007 – No Wyoming Big Sagebrush was recorded where the Aerial Wildlife (Desert Unit) Seeding overlapped drill seedings.  At WNWI – 03 Wyoming Big Sagebrush was recorded at very low density (two plants were recorded.)  No Wyoming Big Sagebrush was recorded at WNWI – 04 or WNWC – 01.  At WNWC – 01 the Desert Unit seeding was monitored where a flight path closely overlapped a concave drainage channel/water receiving area.  Other monitoring plots were located on convex water-shedding uplands.  Landscape position did not seem to make a difference in seeding success. 
2008 – No Wyoming Big Sagebrush was recorded where the Aerial Wildlife (Desert Unit) Seeding overlapped drill seedings.  Since individual quadrat frames are repeatable at these permanent transect locations we can be more confident about changes in recorded densities from year to year at these locations.  During the second year, no Wyoming Big Sagebrush was recorded or observed at WNWI – 03, WNWI – 04, or WNWC – 01.  Minor yearly density fluctuations along paced transects (such as the one recorded at WNWI – 03) should be interpreted with caution because individual quadrats are not absolutely repeatable. 
2009 – Density numbers recorded at individual monitoring plot locations are presented above for reference.  The large array of numbers recorded at all monitoring locations over the three year period might normally confound interpretation, but since only one species (Wyoming Big Sagebrush) was seeded and densities are so low, interpretation is not difficult.  Because the Aerial Wildlife (Desert Unit) Seeding was monitored at numerous separate locations that employed either paced or permanent transects to gather density figures, we may be relatively confident in the monitoring results.  Recorded densities of Wyoming Big Sagebrush were very low throughout the monitoring period at WNWI – 03, WNWC – 01, WNND – 01, WNND – 04, and at WNND – 06.  At paced transect sites (-WI –, -WC –) yearly fluctuations may be regarded cautiously.  At permanent transect sites (“-ND –“) we can be more confident of repeatability.   At WNWI – 04, WNND – 03, WNND – 05, WNND – 07, WNND – 09, and WNND – 10 Wyoming Big Sagebrush was not recorded.  The greatest success recorded (although numbers still never exceeded very low density) was at WNWC – 01.  This monitoring location represented a shallow, U-shaped, second-order drainage overlapped by a flight path.  Other monitoring locations primarily represented convex uplands.  The pattern of success in concave areas and failure on convex areas represented by these plots is supported by observations in the field in areas that were not sampled.  Apparently, the action of unrestricted wind on convex uplands in the treated area transported Wyoming Big Sagebrush into swales.  Patterns were observed where most sagebrush seedlings were present in concave dips and absent from convex rises.  Unfortunately, most sagebrush seedlings observed casually were Basin Big Sagebrush, so the fate of the majority of the Wyoming Big Sagebrush seed applied in the “Desert Unit” seeding remains unknown: it may still remain in the seed bank.  Because Wyoming Big Sagebrush seedlings were observed at very low density across the wide area treated with the “Desert Unit” seeding, we may consider this treatment partially successful, but only marginally so.

Objectives: Establish Wyoming and Basin Big sagebrush on the fire area utilizing aerial seeding techniques.
Planned_Implementation: Unknown
Actual_Implementation:
Wyoming big sagebrush was aerially seeded in strips
over the burned area in December, 2010, as part of the ESR treatments
Approximately 577 acres were aerial seeded with a mixture of basin big and Wyoming big sagebrush. The project was completed in one day on December 15,2010. ESR specialist monitored the activities and conditions.
Contractor, Thomas Helicopter, distributed 8,560 pounds of Wyoming big sagebrush seed using two helicopters with buckets. The contractor started on December 15, 2010 and finished on December 21. Winter conditions prevailed with a partial cover of snow on the ground.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Treatment monitoring
performed in summer 2011 detected sagebrush seedlings primarily in open areas lacking
perennial grass cover. However, seedlings were not detected in areas dominated by previously established
crested wheatgrass seedings. This supplemental planting is proposed to re-establish
Wyoming big sagebrush in areas where shrub seeding was not successful due to competition
from existing plant cover.

Data collected at the end of June from six monitoring sites (see attached map) showed some presence of the seeded species, Wyoming big sagebrush. Of the five belt transect sites two showed a presence of sagebrush, BD001 and BD002, with site BD002 showing the largest amount of Wyoming big sagebrush seedlings. The two monitoring sites are located in the middle third of the fire.
Monitoring site BD005 collected grazing and full ESR data. This site did not detect the presence of sagebrush.
From the photo plots and cover data it appeared the fire area appears to be primarily crested wheatgrass, Sandburg bluegrass, and tumble mustard with cheatgrass encroachment. Cover data taken at monitoring site, BD005, shows bare ground with 56% cover and cheatgrass with 6.7% cover.
Fire ecologists conducted a site visit at the end of August concentrating on the southern half of the fire in the general area of monitoring points BD002, BD003, and BD004. Crested wheatgrass, and sandberg bluegrass were the predominant vegetative cover with only intermittent small pockets of cheatgrass.
Sagebrush seedlings were evident in a wide area of the fire around BD002 and BD003. In areas of heavy crested wheatgrass cover the seedlings were observed only in open areas and where the crested wheat cover was light the seedlings were numerous. At the southern end of the fire the crested wheatgrass cover was very heavy; no sagebrush seedlings could be detected.
It appears that the sagebrush seeding is taking an early hold in the large open areas as well as small pockets but additional time and monitoring is required to determine the full extent of the seeding success.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Aerial Seeding:
The aerial seeding treatment occurred within the Owyhee River Canyon Wilderness Study Area to help maintain land with wilderness characteristics. The 2016 aerial herbicide application, completed the year of the fire in October, was successful in keeping invasive annual grass numbers low, evident in the 2017 photo and Table 7-4. Also, from the same photo there were some perennial plants that survived the fire’s heat. The plants that survived were primarily shallow and deep-rooted bunchgrasses. Bunchgrasses, excluding Sandberg’s bluegrass, had a collective foliar cover of 8%; bluebunch wheatgrass accounted for 7.1% of the total deep rooted perennial bunchgrasses (Tables 7-3 and 7-4). Collectively, the three species of bunchgrass present in 2017 plots had an average density and median diameter of 4.07/m2 and 1.38 inches (Table 7-3). Only the DRPG density objective was met prior to the aerial seeding treatment.
In 2018, plots were revisited after the aerial seeding treatment, completed in December of the previous year. The data displayed in Table 7-3 show an increase for all DRPG measurements (density, diameter, and foliar cover). Both bluebunch wheatgrass and Sandberg’s blue grass increased foliar cover by approximately 3% (Table 7-4) starting the trend in the right direction for meeting the 20% foliar cover objective. The plots completed this year started to detect the encroaching Russian thistle like the drill seeding plots, but the aerial seeding had a lower amount, reflected by the smaller foliar cover of 0.2% (Table 7-4).
In 2019, second year post-treatment, there was a rise in DRPG foliar cover by 10% increasing from 11 to 21% (Table 7-3); coming mostly from bluebunch wheatgrass, a species from the seed mix. Density and median diameter decreased, but that can be due to several factors, like seedlings that did not survive into the second growing season. The objective for density of plants, including seedlings, was still met. The median basal diameter objective has not been achieved over the three years of monitoring data. The noxious weed, Russian thistle, was the dominant herbaceous cover, like what was observed in the drill seeding.
In 2021, third-year post-treatment, the deep-rooted perennial grass foliar cover decreased significantly from the previous down to 13.3% (Table 7-3). With the drop in foliar cover now none of the objectives for the aerial seeding are being met. There is good news, however, in regard to the 11.5% decrease in the cover of the invasive annual, Russian thistle (Figure 7-4).
In 2021, fourth-year post-treatment, the deep-rooted perennial grass foliar cover decreased significantly from the previous down to 13.3% (Table 7-3). With the drop in foliar cover now none of the objectives for the aerial seeding are being met. There is good news, however, regarding the 11.5% decrease in the cover of the invasive annual, Russian thistle (Figure 7-4).

Targeted Control AIM:
In FY 2018 monitoring the natural recovery site there was 0.3% invasive annual grasses, 4.3% deep-rooted
perennial grasses and 23% shallow-rooted bunchgrasses (Table 8-20). The targeted AIM control plot was setup
to provide additional monitoring information that will be used to assess the plot treatment effectiveness and
assist in future land management decisions for the site.

Planned_Implementation: Approximately 156,587 acres will be seeded with sagebrush species appropriate for the site and the forb\r\nseed mix.
Actual_Implementation:
A total of 9,204 acres of the Trimbly fire that burned in 2002 and then again in the 2015 Soda
fire were aerially seeded with Wyoming big sagebrush and forbs (Appendix A: Table A-10-1).
This area was aerially seeded in approximately 100 foot strips covering 50% (5,044 acres) of the
area at double the normal seeding rate shown for Mix 8 ( due to the reduction in acres, and no
reduction in pounds). The rate was doubled due to seeding into an older established seeding
where seeding sagebrush has typically poor results.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Trimbly Fire Area - Aerial Shrub/Forb Seed Mix 8 Winter 2015/2016 – Wyoming Big Sagebrush
In 2020 the density objective for this treatment was not met. Sagebrush seedlings were detected where Aerial Shrub/Forb Seed Mix 8 was applied within the 2002 Trimbly fire boundary; average density across suitable sites was 0.23 seedlings per 10 m\xb2 in 26 plots (Table 8-43). The Trimbly fire burned in 2002 and was drill seeded in the fall of that year with perennial bunch grasses. Large portions of the drill seeding established well. The established perennial grasses within the Trimbly fire boundary likely prevented the sagebrush that was seeded following the Soda fire from establishing on a broad basis. Chaining that was planned for the area following the aerial seeding for the Soda fire was cancelled due to extremely wet soil conditions during the fall of 2015.

In 2020 the density objective for this treatment was met. Sagebrush seedlings were detected where Aerial Shrub/Forb Seed Mix 8 was applied, this does not include the area where the 2002 Trimbly fire and subsequent drill seeding occurred. Average density across suitable sites was 2.2 seedlings per 10 m\xb2 in 631 plots (Table 8-42). Overall the treatment objective was met. See Table 8-37 for results of the aerial seeding within the Trimbly fire boundary.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The goal of aerial seeding was to establish perennial dominated plant communities that will resist
noxious weeds and invasive species establishment, are critical for sage-grouse and big game, and
will help stabilize soils.
As stated in the aerial grass seeding description the fire removed much of the above ground
annual grass biomass and decreased the annual grass seed bank creating open areas that are suitable for
sagebrush establishment. The best opportunity to establish sagebrush is during the first fall/winter
following fire when these conditions occur. It is much more difficult to establish sagebrush by seeding into
existing vegetation. Consequently it is critical that as much of the burned area as possible be aerially
seeded with sagebrush seed fall/winter 2015.

Objectives:
Aerial Grass Mix 1
1. Foliar cover of large statured perennial grasses (excluding Sandberg bluegrass) is an
average of greater than or equal to 20%.
2. Basal diameter of large statured perennial grasses (excluding Sandberg bluegrass) has a
median value of greater than or equal to 3 inches.
3. A qualitative assessment of the fitness and vigor of native and seeded perennial plant species
determines those species to be established. The assessment would include at a minimum the
following factors: 1) Seed head and seed production, 2) Root mass, and lateral and vertical
growth
Planned_Implementation: Approximately 62,808 acres that, due to terrain, are inaccessible to mechanical treatments will be seeded\r\nwith perennial grass species in the fall of 2015.
Actual_Implementation:
Broadcast Seeding #2 contract began on December 8, 2015 and was completed February 3, 2016.
Duration of contract was estimated to be completed in 44 days but it took 58 days to complete
due to weather issues. Weather conditions during time of the seeding were various; clear,
cloudy, foggy, snowy, with temperatures ranging from 3\xb0F to 35\xb0 F, and varied winds. The
second contract consisted of five grass seeding mixes and seven sagebrush forb mixes as
described below. All areas were seeded at 100% coverage with sagebrush and forbs. Species,
percent live seed (PLS), and bulk seed statistics are presented in Appendix A: Tables A-3
through A-11.

Grass Seeding Mix 1
A total of 18,012 acres were aerially seeded in two seeding locations ranging in elevation from
4,600 to 6,300 ft. These areas were seeded at 100% coverage with native grasses (Appendix A:
Table A-3).
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
In 2020 the perennial grass foliar cover objective for this treatment was not met. Mean foliar cover of perennial bunch grasses excluding Sandberg bluegrass in areas seeded with Aerial Grass Mix 1 was 14.7% across all allotments and pastures, more than twice the foliar cover in 2016 but still below the objective (Table 8-29). Foliar cover at 145 plots ranged from 11.9% to 19.8%. Sandberg bluegrass cover within areas treated with Aerial Grass Mix 1 was 13.5%, perennial forb cover was 4.6%, shrub cover was 3.1%, and exotic annual grass cover was 20.4%.

In 2020 the basal diameter objective for this treatment was met. Basal diameter was measured on 724 individual perennial grasses in the Reynolds Creek and Hardtrigger allotments within the Aerial Grass Mix 1 treatment area; measured individuals included both existing and newly seeded grasses (Table 8-35). Median basal diameter of all large statured perennial grasses was 3.0 inches, an increase of 1 inch from 2016.
Reproduction of large statured perennial bunch grasses was assessed in 381 plots sampled in Aerial Grass Mix 1. In 311 of the 312 plots, >75% of the perennial bunch grasses produced seed heads, 50-75% produced seed heads in 44 plots.
////
1. Mean foliar cover of perennial bunch grasses excluding Sandberg bluegrass in areas seeded with
Aerial Grass Mix 1 was 11.0% across all allotments and pastures, nearly double the foliar cover
in 2016 but still 9% below the objective (Table 8-11). Foliar cover at 145 plots ranged from
6.6% in Pasture 3 of the Reynolds Creek allotment to 16.0% in Pasture 5 of the Hardtrigger
allotment. Sandberg bluegrass cover within areas treated with Aerial Grass Mix 1 was 15 .1 %.

2. Basal diameter was measured on 718 individual perennial grasses in the Reynolds Creek and
Hardtrigger allotments within the Aerial Grass Mix 1 treatment area; measured individuals
included both existing and newly seeded grasses (Table 8-17). Median basal diameter of all
large statured perennial grasses was 2.6 in, ranging from 2.1 in to 2.8 in, an increase of 0.6
inches. This treatment objective was not met in 2017.

3. Aerial Grass Mix 1
Reproduction of large statured perennial bunch grasses was assessed in 184 plots sampled in
Aerial Grass Mix 1. Of the 184 plots, 133 plots exhibited >75% seed head production.

Actual_Implementation: A total of 5,974 acres were aerially seeded near active greater sage-grouse leks in 2017 in Coal\r\nMine Basin, Shares Basin, and Rockville Pasture 7 lek area ranging in elevation from 4,000 to\r\n5,200 ft. These areas were seeded at 100% coverage (Appendix A: Table A-25).
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
In 2019 and 2020 the areas seeded with the sage-grouse preferred forb mix were surveyed for all plant species using meandering transects within each seeded polygon for Rockville Pasture 7, Shares Basin Pasture 1, Blackstock Springs 1 and Succor Creek Pasture 1. While native forb richness and abundance were moderate to high in these areas, (11 native forb species in Shares Basin 1 to 27 in Rockville 7) the only species found that were in the sage-grouse preferred seed mix were Balsamorhiza sagittata, Astragalus filipies, and Crepis occidentalis, which may or may not have originated from the seeding.

In 2017, the areas seeded with sage-grouse preferred forb mix were surveyed for all plant species
using meandering transects within each seeded polygon. Plant species were recorded throughout
each transect while targeting the seeded sage-grouse preferred forbs. All seeded species were
located in at least one of the four seeding areas. Penstemon eatonii was found in the highest
quantities but never approached the objective of 0.5 plants per 10 m2 in suitable areas. Most
Lomatium dissectum, Crepis occidentalis, Balsamorhiza sagittata and Astragalus filipies
individuals that were observed were established plants that were likely not the result of the aerial
seeding, although a few A. filipies seedlings were found in the aerially seeded portion of the
Succor Creek allotment. Penstemon accuminatus and Dalea ornata were found within the
seeded portion of Shares Basin in Shares Basin Pasture 1 and Hardtrigger Pasture 4.
The aerially seeded portion of Sands Basin Pasture 4 had the highest number and quantity of
sage-grouse preferred forbs and is closest to meeting the objective. This is likely because this
area had the most suitable areas for seed germination, i.e. areas where shrubs were present before
the Soda fire and therefore burned hot leaving bare soil. This area also is in a Loamy 11-13
ecological site and therefore has consistently deeper soils than the other areas that were seeded
with this mix. Six of the ten seeded species were found in this area; A. filipies, B. sagittata, C.
occidentalis, Malacothrix glabrata, P. eatonii, and Sphaeralcea spp. Where seeded species were
found they exceeded the objective but seeded forbs were not found in all suitable areas.
In 2016, it is likely that the individual forbs detected during monitoring were plants that existed
prior to the Soda fire and not as a result of the seeding. Crepis was detected in 13 pastures and
B. sagittata was detected in 12 of the 14 pastures monitored. A. filipies was detected in half of
the 14 pastures. Penstemon, Malacothrix, and Sphaeralcea were not detected in any of the
pastures. The Jackson Creek allotment had the highest density of B. sagittata and second highest
of Crepis; all pastures monitored in this allotment were treated with aerial herbicide during the
spring of 2016 (see Part 6, S5 for details).

2. Plant phenology was not assessed in 2016. In 2017 the majority of the emerged seeded perennial
forbs were either flowering or fruiting at the time of monitoring.

Objectives:
The objective is to prevent sagebrush communities to transitioning into an annual plant state and restoring essential forage and cover for greater sage grouse.

1. Obtain an average of 1 seeded plant per meter\xb2 by the end of the fifth year following fire incident, which occurred on 07/30/2016.
2. Obtain 100% or greater perennial cover of the low potential perennial plant cover for the appropriate ecological site by the end of the fifth year following fire containment.
3. The aerial seeding would result in lower abundance (density and cover) of invasive annual plant species, and a higher abundance of desirable perennial plant species than the unseeded control area.
4. Seeded species would be well established and reproducing.
Planned_Implementation:
The BLM proposes to aerially seed a total of 3,900 acres of public land managed by
BLM that was burned by the Poodle fire. Seeding would occur in the fall or winter with a
preference for application in late fall or early winter. The possible species the project
would be seeded with are biuebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata spp. spicata),
Squirreltail (Elymus elymoides), Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda), sulphur buckwheat
(Eriogonum umbellatum), Low sagebrush (Artemisia arbuscular) and Tapertip
Hawksbeard (Crepis acuminata).
Actual_Implementation: Aerial seed 3,900 acres with a seed mix containing native, perennial grasses, forbs, and sagebrush.

Objectives: The objectives for cover will be to obtain 70% of all perennial plant cover found in the associated reference site, or, when not possible, achieve 50% of the lowest value for perennial cover associated with the appropriate ecological or range site by the need of the third year. Density objectives for aerially seeded areas will be based on having one seeded species firmly rooted per square meter by first or second growing season following seeding.
Planned_Implementation: Aerial seeding was vital in mitigating the potential loss of Greater sage grouse habitat in the Montana, Granite, and Bilk Creek mountain ranges. Without treatment the burned areas are extremely susceptible to exotic annual dominance; this would jeopardize the Greater sage grouse, mule deer herds and other wildlife that depend on this area year-round and especially in the winter months. The areas selected are predominantly upland areas where topography is unsuitable for drill seeding due to slope and accessibility. All aerial seeding occurred in sage grouse PPH or PGH that was severely burned. Sage grouse habitat in the Bilk, Trout Creek, and Montana Mountains is widely regarded as being exceptionally productive when compared with other areas designated as sage grouse PPH. The application cost of aerial seeding is fairly high, but the risk of not seeding is the loss of species and structural diversity that will reduce the overall short and long-term value of the land.
Actual_Implementation: Mike Whalen Project Inspector. The area was aerially seeded using a helicopter with\r\nmountain sagebrush seed (Artemisia tridentata ssp. vaseyana). Refer to map 4 and table 4 in\r\npart 12 Attachments.

Objectives: Goal: Increase diversity of desirable grasses, forbs, and shrubs to preserve and maintain habitat for sensitive\r\nwildlife species, as well as prevent erosion in susceptible areas.
Planned_Implementation:
Seed mixtures comprised of native shrubs and stabilizing mixes of native grasses would be
aerial broadcast seeded.  Aerial seeding of shrubs is proposed as an ES treatment to augment
the development of vegetative structure across the burned landscape to further reduce
sediment movement from wind and water erosion, which will aid in restoring habitat for
sage-grouse and several other BLM sensitive wildlife species associated with the sagebrush
steppe. The area was also important habitat for bighorn sheep and is utilized by mule deer
and antelope.
Actual_Implementation: 1 mix of sagebrush at 70% area\r\ncoverage (375\u2019 swath width) in non- wilderness 6,392 acres.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Objectives and Results
1. Attain a density of 1 sagebrush seedling per 10m\xb2 in suitable areas. Conduct density
monitoring.
This objective was met in 2015 due to the reseeding in February of 2014. In August of 2015, in
suitable sites, six transects of density hoop monitoring were conducted in areas that were aerially
seeded with sagebrush. Locations seeded with Wyoming big sagebrush were meeting the
objective with a density of 7.1 seedlings per 10m2. Low sagebrush seeding areas (Artemisia
arbuscula) were not monitored.
Large patches of sagebrush seedlings were noted at grass monitoring plots 1-2, 1-2, 2-3, 2-5, 4-1,
and 5-1, and in the wilderness plot 3-1. Seedlings were 1-18” in height and appeared healthy;
many were beginning to flower. Trace amounts of sagebrush were found in areas seeded with
low sagebrush.
2. Attain a density of 2.5 perennial seeded grass plants per square meter (in
grass/sagebrush seed mix non-wilderness area). Conduct density monitoring.
Site assessments were conducted in areas favorable for germination and establishment of
perennial seeded grasses. No seedlings were observed in 2013, even in highly suitable areas
where terrain would have naturally collected seed (e.g., crevices, near drainages).
Overall, this objective was met. Areas seeded with Mix 1 in 2013 were surveyed for Sandberg
bluegrass and Idaho fescue grass density in 2015. Seeded grass density ranged from 1 to 22
Sandberg bluegrass plants per 1 m2 and 0 to 8 Idaho fescue plants per 1 m2. Idaho fescue plants
were noted in 5 quadrats of 9 total quadrats surveyed.
3. 80% of canopy gaps less than 50cm. Conduct canopy gap monitoring.
After three years of growth it is unrealistic to expect aerially seeded grass to be large enough to
reduce gap size. Therefore, this objective has been disregarded.


ESR Monitoring Report 2022
S3 Aerial Seeding 
Treatment(s) 
Pockets of suitable planting sites, areas where the seeded species would typically grow under normal conditions, were present across fire perimeter. Suitable sites are often difficult to delineate post-fire, covering the entire area better ensured all suitable sites were seeded. 
Contractors initially seeded 14,569 acres by helicopter on January 19, 2013; 473 acres were seeded with the grass/sagebrush mix- mix 1 (100% coverage), 6,392 acres were seeded with the forb/sagebrush mix - mix 2 (70% coverage - 375’ swath width), and 7,704 acres were seeded with the sagebrush mix - mix 3 (100% coverage). Aerial seeding density was not conducted in 2013; however, ESR personnel made numerous site visits to look for germination of seeded species during installation of vegetation recovery monitoring plots. Seven of the eleven 
Contractors re-treated 6,835 acres on February 27, 2014 (see re-treatment rationale for more information). Wyoming big sagebrush was seeded by helicopter (50% coverage – 250’ swath width, skip seeding). 

2014 Aerial Seeding Mix
Sagebrush density monitoring was not conducted in 2017. 
This objective was met in 2015 due to the reseeding in February of 2014. In August of 2015, in suitable sites, six transects of density hoop monitoring were conducted in areas that were aerially seeded with sagebrush. Locations seeded with Wyoming big sagebrush were meeting the objective with a density of 7.1 seedlings per 10m2. Low sagebrush seeding areas (Artemisia arbuscula) were not monitored. 
Large patches of sagebrush seedlings were noted at grass monitoring plots 1-2, 1-2, 2-3, 2-5, 4-1, and 5-1, and in the wilderness plot 3-1. Seedlings were 1-18” in height and appeared healthy; many were beginning to flower. Trace amounts of sagebrush were found in areas seeded with low sagebrush.

Grass density monitoring was not conducted in 2017. 
Site assessments were conducted in areas favorable for germination and establishment of perennial seeded grasses. No seedlings were observed in 2013, even in highly suitable areas where terrain would have naturally collected seed (e.g., crevices, near drainages). 
Overall, this objective was met in 2015. Areas seeded with Mix 1 in 2013 were surveyed for Sandberg bluegrass and Idaho fescue grass density in 2015. Seeded grass density ranged from 1 to 22 Sandberg bluegrass plants per 1 m2 and 0 to 8 Idaho fescue plants per 1 m2. Idaho fescue plants were noted in 5 quadrats of 9 total quadrats surveyed.

Canopy gap of aerially seeded species was not conducted in 2017.

Other Results 
In late June 2022, ESR staff qualitatively monitored four plots. 
The aspen (Populus tremuloides) stand at plot G1MKPPASP1 showed very good recovery with trees 6-8 feet tall (photo below). Snowbrush ceanothus (Ceanothus velutinus) was in poor condition due to heavy browse by elk. Due to landscape position and elevation snow sits longer at this plot. Plant phenology was a few weeks behind communities in the flat; bottlebrush squirreltail (Elymus elymoides) was just beginning to bloom on June 29th. Yarrow (Achillea millefolium) was abundant across the site. Large patches of bare soil persist but they have not filled in with either cheatgrass or noxious weeds. Though a few shrubs have resprouted, the area is functionally a grassland.

A former low sagebrush (Artemisia arbuscula) site, the plant community at plot G1MKT02 is now primarily Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda), bluebunch wheatgrass (Psuedoroegneria spicata) and bottlebrush squirreltail (photos below). Many of the bluebunch bases had dead inner cores which may have occurred due to the drought in 2021. A handful of sagebrush seedlings were found. Forb diversity included lava aster (Ionactis alpina), lupine (Lupinus sp.), willowherb (Epilobium brachycarpum), hawksbeard (Crepis sp.), pale agoseris (Agoseris glauca), hatless daisy (Erigeron aphanactis), and longleaf phlox (Phlox longifolia). Sandberg bluegrass was subdominant (10-40% abundance) across the site interspersed with small gravel.

Plot G1MKT05 falls in a small draw in Owens Pasture 1 which was representative of draws within the pasture. The plot was heavily invaded with cheatgrass and tall tumblemustard (Sisimbrium altissimum) (photos below). Bottlebrush squirreltail and yellow rabbitbrush (Chrysothamnus viscidiflorus) were present at low abundance. A few crested wheatgrass (Agropyron cristatum) plants were also noted at this plot.

G1MKNT04 was not treated as part of the Jacks ESR plan. Sandberg bluegrass and bottlebrush squirreltail have recovered well though cheatgrass fills interspaces in the gravel soil surface in 2022.

RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS 
Canopy gap objectives were not met in either Owens or Northwest allotments though most pastures were within 6% of the objective. Invasive non-native annuals have increased significantly at some plots, particularly in pasture 12 of the Northwest allotment. Perennial grasses have increased in size since 2013, were producing seed heads and plants were in good vigor. Overall, site assessments and photos indicate that perennial grasses have recovered in both treated and natural recovery areas. Grazing was resumed in Owens Allotment in June 2015 (see Part 12: Additional Information). Monitoring ten years post-fire shows very good grass recovery across the burned area. Though there are some patches of cheatgrass present, no large expanses occur in the fire perimeter. 
The aerial sagebrush seeding objective was met in 2015 due to the reseeding in February of 2014. Moisture in February and March of 2014 were above average as was late summer and fall moisture; this likely helped with the establishment and growth of the seeded sagebrush. Sagebrush seedlings may have been missed or not yet germinated and emerged during monitoring in 2014 but were picked up during monitoring of 2015. Few sagebrush seedlings were found during ten-year monitoring in 2022. Much of the Jacks fire is now functionally a grassland. 
Canada thistle is common throughout the Big Jacks Creek riparian corridor and due its extent, chemical treatment will not be implemented. These sites will be targeted for biological control releases in the future. A population of Scotch thistle detected at the reservoir in 2014 was treated in 2015. It is expected this treatment will be effective but both sites will require continued monitoring to prevent re-establishment. Although the most likely areas for invasion have been inventoried, continued monitoring of treatment sites and the burned area is recommended. Continued monitoring should focus on travel corridors and highly disturbed sites

The Point Fire started as a lightning strike on July 1, 2013. The Fire grew rapidly due to erratic
winds, steep and inaccessible terrain. The Fire burned a total of 2,948 acres in Twin Falls County
approximately eight miles south of Rogerson, Idaho. Of those burned acres, 2,782 acres occurred

and a portion of Pasture Mc 1 of the Mule Creek PVGA allotment (129 acres). The elevation
throughout the Fire varied between 5,500 to 6,500 feet. A large portion of the burned area is
inaccessible because of the steep slopes and cliff areas. The burned area’s topography is
characterized as rocky steep slopes, steep draws and ridges. In some areas of the burn, slopes
range from 30-60 percent.
The Fire burned within a variety of vegetation communities; mid to late seral sagebrush
(Mountain and Wyoming big sagebrush, low sagebrush and Antelope bitterbrush) steppe
communities. Past fires on the same mountain range have demonstrated the potential conditions
if rehabilitated and not rehabilitated. The Fire burned quickly with highest severity in steep
draws of sagebrush and bitterbrush.

FY 17
Monitoring plots were revisited for the 5th year monitoring by Chicago Botanical interns in the summer of 2017. Qualitative assessments were completed and included a general plot description, species inventory, and photo documentation. For the 5th year monitoring year, seven plots were revisited for qualitative assessments. Plots visited include 001, 002, 004, 006, 009, 010, and 012.
The Kinyon Road rehabilitation can be addressed geographically, as the treatments were divided separately into the eastern and western burned areas. The focus of this summary will be on the west side, also known as the Bruneau Overlook area, as heavy noxious weed infestations and unsuccessful drill seedings here were concerning. Due to the good establishment of the drill seed treatments on the eastern side, attention and resources should be focused on the Bruneau Overlook area in future treatments.
On the eastern side of Kinyon, drill seedings were highly successful. Perennial grasses, particularly bluebunch wheatgrass and Siberian wheatgrass, dominate the landscape, and the bare ground among them supports a high diversity of forbs with relatively low cheatgrass establishment. Though sagebrush seedlings were either not found or found in extremely low amounts in these areas, many sagebrush islands were seen near monitoring points, and could potentially re-seed the area regardless of the success of shrub seedings. Invasive weeds such as rush skeletonweed, halogeton, and Russian thistle are present, but are not an imminent threat, especially considering the health and expanse of the perennial grasses. It would be valuable for future projects to assess why the eastern Kinyon plantings were so successful compared to the Bruneau Overlook area.
The Bruneau Overlook seeding treatments have been moderately successful but present several challenges. In some areas, drill-seeded perennial bunchgrass populations are vigorous and extensive with good forb diversity, but cheatgrass density is still high. Most areas on this side of the Kinyon fire are cheatgrass-Sandberg’s bluegrass dominated sites with low forb diversity, and drill-seeded perennials are not competing as well. Few to no sagebrush seedlings were seen across the area, and sagebrush islands were also rarer. Noxious and invasive weed populations also present a problem.
A main concern for this area is extremely dense invasive weed populations, particularly Russian thistle. The Bruneau Overlook area is being overtaken by this dominant weed, and full hillsides of robust Russian thistle were found near monitoring points (Photo 1). The eastern monitoring area also showed some large Russian thistle populations. Russian thistle is likely to continue dominating the Kinyon Road area unless significant control measures are taken. Rush skeletonweed is also present across the Kinyon Road fire area, though to a much lesser extent than the thistle. It has the potential to continue spreading and impeding the advancement of perennial bunchgrasses. Chemical treatments in the Bruneau Overlook area on Russian thistle and rush skeletonweed would be most efficient in stopping the spread of these two species, though mechanical treatments on extremely dense Russian thistle patches could also be valuable.
Kinyon Road Fire (G1CH) FY2022 Monitoring – 10th Year 33
Precipitation data is from the Twin Buttes and Horse Butte RAWS stations, which are northeast of the burned area and southwest of the burned area, respectively. Monitoring reports at the first, second- and third-year mark illuminate a trend towards higher precipitation following treatment years, along with later summer and fall rains. This factor may have contributed to higher weed establishment and lower drill seed success. Previous reports also mention soil movement that filled in drill rows and lessened the establishment rate at Bruneau Overlook sites. Compounding this was the inefficient depth band use on the shrub seedings, consequently the first three years of monitoring found no shrub establishment in the monitoring sites. Upon qualitative monitoring at the five-year mark, scattered immature Wyoming big sagebrush were found in only half of the monitoring sites for all of Kinyon. Multiple factors led to both the low shrub establishment throughout Kinyon and the partial success of drill seed treatments in Bruneau Overlook.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
To re-establish sagebrush for wildlife habitat and perennial cover
The Coonskin Fire ignited in the central Jarbidge Field Office on July 31, 2013. Fire cause was
lightning. The fire was contained on August 1 and controlled on August 2. The fire burned 4,378
acres of public land administered by the BLM.
The fire burned 3,872 acres of Sage-grouse Preliminary Priority Habitat (PPH). Within the Sagegrouse
PPH, 128 acres were classified as key habitat dominated by sagebrush communities and
3,744 acres were R1 restoration habitat dominated by perennial grasslands. The entire area
burned in 2008 in the Murphy Complex Fire. Sagebrush islands left by that fire burned in the
Coonskin Fire.
The burned area is surrounded by sage-grouse leks. Three occupied sage-grouse leks occur 0.8,
3.7, and 5.2 miles from the fire perimeter. Numbers of sage-grouse attending these leks has
declined following wildfires in the area since the mid-1990s. Three status undetermined sagegrouse
leks occur 0.8, 1.0, and 1.3 miles from the burned area. The area is used by sage-grouse
for nesting. Occupied pygmy rabbit (a candidate species) is less than 1.0 mile from the west side
of the fire. Ferruginous hawk and prairie falcon (both BLM sensitive species) hunt small
mammals in the area, but nesting habitat is 2.0 to 2.5 miles to the east and southeast. Prior to the
fire the area was used by pronghorn for fawning. The fire burned big game winter range.
Wintering big game include pronghorn, elk and mule deer.

Resource management objectives for the affected MUAs:
Improve lands in poor ecological condition (p. II-47).
Manage big game habitat to support mule deer and antelope (p. II-48).
Improve sage-grouse habitat (p. II-48).

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The Lost Fire occurred on the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) Northern California District
(NOD), Surprise Field Office (SFO) area. It was one of 7 fires that started on the 5th of August
in NOD by lightning. The fire was located approximately 21 miles east/southeast of the town of
Eagleville, CA. The fire started approximately 1 mile north of the Lost Creek Road near the Los
Angeles Department of Water and Power twin 500 KV power lines. When first reported by a
Nevada Department of Wildlife employee, the fire was estimated between 500 – 800 acres in
size and growing. During the initial time period, the SFO Surprise Valley Fire Station was
fighting several new lightning fires. Initial attack suppression forces were dispatched by the
Susanville Interagency Dispatch Center and Jerry Wheeler DC-3206 assumed the role as Lost
Incident Commander. Around the time of ignition, surface winds increased from the southwest
and ranged from 5 to 8 mph with gusts up to 15 mph. On August 5th, a ridge of high pressure
over the Four Corners region intensified while a thermal trough developed over central Nevada.
The combination of these two climatic features increased heating and resulted in the
development of an extremely dry air mass over the fire area. High temperatures were 5 to 8
degrees above normal and ranged from 92 to 97 degrees. Corresponding minimum relative
humidity (RH) values dropped to 5-9 percent. The lowest RH recorded during the fire was 2
percent. On August 5th, the fire exceeded the capabilities of initial response efforts and the fire
burned through the evening and was estimated to be approximately 9,000 acres by the morning
of August 6th. During the afternoon and evening of August 6th and 7th, the fire made significant
runs to the east and northeast, consuming approximately 15,000 acres each day. On August 8th,
the fire spread primarily northeast and southeast following fuels and terrain for another 15,000
acres. Suppression actions and a major change in fuel type reduced fire spread on August 9th, but
the fire area still increased in size by approximately 3,900 acres. The fire was contained on
August 12th at approximately 61,537 acres.

delineated. This information was also used to determine appropriate seed mixes. Seeded species
are based on site potential, while considering seed availability and cost. In addition, specific
cultivars of the species chosen were selected based on seedling vigor and ability to germinate
and persist on low precipitation sites. Consideration was also given to vegetation structural

BLM staff identified the areas within the burn where habitat values for sage-grouse were highly
impacted and special emphasis was placed on restoring native vegetation to these areas. High
priority areas were primarily higher elevation nesting and summer habitat. In addition, the AFO
staff also worked with the Natural Resource Conservation Service (NRCS) in Reno and
Professor Stringham form the University of Nevada-Reno (UNR) to develop seed mixes that
would be appropriate based on site conditions. Hand planting and aerial seeding sites were also
delineated using the same methodology.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Aerial Mix A Seeding
Density Results 
Rehabilitation objectives of are considered successfully met when one native forb per square meter and 0.3 native shrubs per square meter are established. 
2018: Rehabilitation objectives in the first growing season have not been met. The site’s native regrowth has been very successful, but the seeded species are showing unimpressive progress towards success, especially the seeded forbs, which were not found to be establishing in the first growing season. 
2019: It is noteworthy that native perennial grass recovery is abundant. However, the lack of seeding establishment is unexpected given the improved weather conditions over the past year.
2020: Minimal seeded western yarrow was observed while no seeded sagebrush was observed. The recovery of small and large-form grasses was evident on the site but largely reduced from the 2019 season observations. 
2022: No seeded species were observed during density data collection. Native regrowth of small form grass species remained abundant but still declined from 2020 by nearly half. Native forb growth was fairly high at 3.9/m2 and shrub regrowth was moderate at 0.8/m2. 
AIM Data Results 
Cover 
2018: The foliar cover eclipsed bare ground in the first growing season, which indicates the first year regrowth success. The foliar cover was comprised of 70.7% perennial grass cover. Perennial grasses and shrubs (1.3% cover) were winning ground against annual, invasive cheatgrass (46.7%). Perennial forbs will benefit from higher precipitation in the second growing season as they have only attainted 6.7% cover so far 
2019: The foliar cover was dominated by perennial grasses (78.7%) which is an improvement from the previous year’s observations. Annual grasses reduced by half compared to 2018 results (23.3%). There was a decrease in annual forb observations. 
2020: Foliar cover reduced dramatically from years before, with the largest reduction being observed in perennial and annual grasses with smaller reductions throughout each of the indicators. 
2022: Foliar cover was moderately high at 77.3%, an increase of 25.4% from 2020. Perennial grasses increased to 43.2% from 34.7% in 2020. In conjunction with the decrease of cheatgrass by 0.6% and annual forbs by 9.6%, the increase in perennial grasses, perennial forbs, and shrubs, the health of this plot appears to have improved since 2020.
Gaps and Erosion 
2018: Gaps in canopy cover were infrequent and short. Canopy gaps of the size and frequency measured on the plots have not allowed wind and water erosion to occur. The hydrologic function and soil and site stability have not been impacted due to the near 90% canopy cover. Wind and water erosion were minimally affecting the soil and site stability on the plot: there few pedestals were present in 2018. 
2019: Canopy gaps were mostly between 25 and 50 cm long. This is similar to 2018 observations. A reduction in pedestalling and water flow patterns was observed, indicating more stability on the site. 
2020: The majority of canopy gaps remained in the category of 25cm - 50cm long. This is consistent with data from the 2018 and 2019 seasons. Similar rare pedestalling and deposition/runoff were observed on the site. This indicates stability on the site. 
2022: Gaps increased in the 25-50cm and the 51-100cm ranges greatly since 2022 but the continued decline of annuals species observed on the plot alongside the lack of soil instability and site erosion observed on the plot does not cause a lot of concern at this time.
Species Richness
2022: Species richness did decrease by 5 species since 2020, most concerning is the loss of 3 perennial grasses but there was also an increase of one shrub species with none of the annual species increasing.
Recommendations: 
2018: Monitoring results in the treatment area have shown that rehabilitation objectives have not been met in the first growing season. Although the relatively high precipitation zone areas have seen robust regrowth of native perennials post-fire, the seeded forbs and shrubs have not successfully established and the area needs to remain closed. If the upcoming winter and second year growing season receive normal to above normal precipitation and snowpack is maintained by cooler winter temperatures, the seeded species have a higher chance at establishing and meeting rehabilitation objectives. Since the regrowth of native, perennial forbs was so low, the area would benefit from the forb-seeding establishment, as well as the seeded sagebrush. 
2019: Monitoring results in the treatment area have shown that rehabilitation objectives have not been met in the second growing season. No seeded forbs were observed and a reduced amount of seeded shrubs were observed. This is unexpected given more normal temperatures and increased precipitation in the area. The native recovery for grasses on the site is noteworthy. There was and allotment closure issued for the Gamble Individual allotment in the East Delano Mountain pasture. It is advised that the area receives additional rest as it would benefit from the forb-seeding establishment, as well as the seeded sagebrush. 
2020: Monitoring results in the treatment area have shown that rehabilitation objectives have not been met in the third growing season. No seeded forbs or shrubs were observed. The native recovery for grasses on the site is noteworthy. There was and allotment closure issued for the Gamble Individual allotment in the East Delano Mountain pasture. It is advised that the area receives additional rest as it would benefit from the forb-seeding establishment, as well as the seeded sagebrush. 
2022: Monitoring results in the treatment area have shown that the rehabilitation objectives still have not been met. No seeded species were observed during density but some native regrowth has been observed and show promise of future establishment on the plot. There was and allotment closure issued for the Gamble Individual allotment in the East Delano Mountain pasture. It is advised that the area receives additional rest as it would benefit from the forb-seeding establishment, as well as the seeded sagebrush.

Density Results: 
Rehabilitation objectives will be considered met when one seeded forb, 0.3 seeded shrubs, and three seeded grasses per square meter are observed.

The aerially seeded grasses and forbs had the biggest successes in AIM Plot 08, which is a higher elevation pinyon pine and juniper site. Forbs have had a small amount of success by establishing at a density of 0.2 plants per square meter and seeded grasses have established at a density of 0.58 plants per square meter. 
2019: In 2019 monitoring results, a higher amount of seeded grasses were observed. This primarily was due to observations of Sandberg’s bluegrass which could also be considered part of native recovery on the site. Some seeded Wyoming big sagebrush was observed with an increase in large-form and decrease in small-form species as well. The small amount of seeded species establishment and native recovery is somewhat unexpected for the site given the improvement in weather over the past year. 
2020: No seeded shrubs were observed. Some seeded forbs were observed and seeded grasses were observed in abundance. Recovery of large and small-form perennial grasses was also observed. 
2022: Rehabilitation objectives for this plot have not been fully met. Shrubs and grasses meet the criteria with 0.7/m2 and 18.9/m2 observed but forbs fell short at 0.1. However, native regrowth of shrubs shows signs of establishment at 2.8/m2 along with shrubs at 0.8/m2. 
AIM Data Results: 
Cover 
2018: The bare ground was more prevalent than foliar cover by 34.7% in the first growing season, which indicates that more time is necessary for rest and growth. The foliar cover was comprised of 15.3% native, perennial grass cover. Tree cover represented 10.0% foliar cover. Perennial forbs and shrubs will benefit from higher precipitation in the second growing season as they were not observed this season. 
2019: Foliar cover was dominated by perennial grasses (44.7%), primarily due to Sandberg’s bluegrass (14.9%) and Siberian wheatgrass (8.2%) observations, similar to 2018 results. Second to this was the annual forb observations (24.7%) with desert madwort and prickly lettuce making up 8.4% and 5.8% of foliar cover. Halogeton, an invasive species, was observed on the plots and made up 5.1% foliar cover. Tree cover was reduced from 2018 observations to 3.3% cover. 
2020: Cover was moderately low. Cover was dominated by perennial Siberian wheatgrass and Sandberg bluegrass and annual wheatgrass. Cheatgrass was observed on the site with low cover (4.7%) along with desert madwort (2.2%). Collectively, perennial species dominated cover over annual species on the sites. 
2022: Cover was moderate at 60.0%, dominated by perennial grasses (19.8%), followed by annual forbs (8.3), and annual grass reducing from 4.7% in 2020 to 3.2% in 2022. Most indicators saw a reduction in cover with perennial grasses taking the biggest hit, losing around 15% of its cover.

Gaps and Erosion 
2018: Gaps in canopy cover were long and frequently occurring, allowing wind and water erosion to occur. The hydrologic function and soil and site stability have been impacted due to these gaps and the lack of perennial canopy cover on the sites. Very short and rare water flow patterns, common pedestals, few and short rills, and rare soil deposition/runoff gave proof of the impaired soil and site stability in 2018. 
2019: Gaps remained very similar to results from the 2018 season. Although canopy cover has increased significantly, gaps are still common enough to make the site susceptible to wind and water erosion. In 2019 observations, there were decreased observations of rills, similar observations of common pedestalling and water flow patterns, and increased observations of common deposition/runoff. This indicates soil instability on the site. 
2020: Gaps decreased across all ranges and were primarily between 51 and 100 cm long. Fewer pedestals were observed along with no deposition/runoff and no water flow patterns. This indicates increased stability on the site. 
2022: Gaps increased in each size range; the bottom 3 size classes saw the largest increases with >200cm only seeing an increase of 2.2% from 0.6% last year. The reduction of foliar cover across the plot likely had an impact on gap increasing across the plot but a lack of soil instability and plot degradation across the plot means the gap increase may not be a bad sign of rehabilitation.
Species Richness
2022: Species richness increased from 2019 from 31 individual species observed to 36. Perennial forbs and shrubs increased while annual forbs reduced by 2. Perennial grasses remained the same and perennials overall continued to outnumber the annuals observed.
Recommendations 
2018: The seeded forbs, grasses, and shrubs have not successfully established and the area needs to remain closed for another growing season or two. If the upcoming winter and second year growing season receive normal to above normal precipitation and snowpack is maintained by cooler winter temperatures, the seeded species have a higher chance at establishing and meeting rehabilitation objectives. Since the regrowth of native, perennial forbs was so low, the area would benefit from the seeded forb establishment, as well as the seeded sagebrush. 
2019: The seeded forbs, grasses, and shrubs have not successfully established. An allotment closure has been issued for the Gamble Individual allotment in the East Delano Mountain pasture. The allotment closure objective of three perennial species per square meter has been met but it is advised that the area receives additional rest. The improved weather conditions did not appear to help the seeded species establishment. Since the regrowth of native, perennial forbs was so low, the area would benefit from the seeded forb establishment, as well as the seeded sagebrush, to provide various wildlife forage. 
2020: Seeded grasses have successfully established on the plot. However, seeded forbs and shrubs still need more time to come in. An allotment closure has been issued for the Gamble Individual allotment in the East Delano Mountain. The allotment closure objective of three perennial species per square meter has been met but it is advised that the area receives proper grazing management so that seeded species may have more of a chance to grow back in. 
2022: Seeded grasses continue to show signs of establishment on the plot and seeded shrubs and forbs show signs of beginning to establish on the plot. The overall health of this site appears positive but continued appropriate grazing management is recommended to allow forbs and shrubs more time to fully establish roots if possible.

The grasses have not developed deep roots, however and the area needs to be rested until the plants achieve more robust basal and canopy growth. The insufficient snowpack and drought-like summer conditions may have contributed to the inability of the shrubs to establish in the area. 
2019: No seeded species were observed. Notably, seeded bitterbrush were also not observed this year. This is unexpected given the improved weather conditions over the past year. 
2020: Seeded grasses were observed. Bluebunch wheatgrass was the primary observed seeded grass. There were no other seeded species observed through density.

Cover
