Draw pasture where Plot 20 is located. The allotment closure objective of three perennial species per square meter was met but it is advised that the area continues to receive proper grazing management so seeded species may establish.

S3 Aerial Mid-Elevation, Imazapic
Density Results
Rehabilitation objectives are considered successfully met when one native forb per square meter and 0.3 native shrubs per square meter per square meter are established.
2022: Rehabilitation objectives have not been met for this treatment though this is the closest to achieving the goals since monitoring began in 2018. Native regrowth is relatively low as well which could indicate that vegetation seeded and unseeded is struggling to rehabilitate.
AIM Data Results
Cover
2022: Total foliar cover was moderately low at 34.0%, dominated by perennial grasses at 19.1%. The next highest coverage came from annual grasses at 3.6% then perennial forbs at 1.3%, none of the other indicators were observed during the Line-Point Intercept data collection method. While it is not ideal to have such low coverage overall, the large decrease of annual grass cover and maintenance of perennial grass cover is a good sign for the health of the plot.
Gaps and Erosion
2018: Wind and water erosion were minimally affecting the soil and site stability on the plot: there were only short and rare water flow patterns and few pedestals.
2019: Similar (rare) observations of deposition/runoff were made along with increased (common) pedestalling and water flow patterns. This suggests more water erosion on the site and slight changes in soil stability.
2020: Similar common pedestalling and rare deposition/runoff but no water flow patterns were observed on the site, indicating increased site stability.
2022: Canopy gap cover increased significantly from 2020 to 2022, the most concerning being the increase of gaps >200cm from 0.0% to 48.8%, along with the increase of gaps 101-200cm from 0.7% to 21.1%. This large increase in gaps in conjunction with the decreased foliar cover and common waterflow patterns observed on the plot are indicators of soil erosion and plot degradation.
Species Richness
2022: Species richness was moderate on the plot with 23 individual species identified. Perennial species increased by 6 species while annual species decreased by one, meaning that perennial species continue to outnumber the annuals.
Recommendations
2022: Monitoring results in the treatment area have shown that rehabilitation objectives have not been met and that native regrowth of the area does not compensate for the lack of seeded species success. Objectives: Aerial Seeding/S3: Objective 2 of the FMDA\u2019s objective and management actions is to maintain, protect, and expand sage grouse source habitats. Following wildland fire, use seeding treatments with appropriate plant materials to attempt to stabilize sites and prevent dominance of invasive, annual vegetation, and noxious weeds. Therefore aerial seeding meets this objective and is in conformance with the RMP as amended by the FMDA.
Planned_Implementation: The majority of the burned BLM land was identified to be aerial seeded with a mixture of native and native like perennial grass and native shrub species. This is proposed to be accomplished in late FY12 or early FY13.
Actual_Implementation: This project consisted of aerial seeding 385 acres within the Hot Well fire of 2012. Rate of application was approximately 1.04 pounds bulk seed per acre. The seed consisted of 400 pounds of Basin Big Sagebrush. The area received a considerable amount of precipitation the following days after seed application. The contractor was Thomas Helicopters, Inc of Gooding, ID. Pilot for the seeding was Rod Thomas. The project was completed using one helicopter and one sling type bucket. The project was started and completed on December 18, 2014.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
The majority of the fire was characterized by moderate to high fire intensity. This was due to a combination of topography and terrain, extremely low fuel moisture and hot and dry weather conditions. Vegetation in the fire area was primarily a phase 2 of phase 3 Utah juniper site, sagebrush and Sandberg bluegrass mix. Areas with a dense overstory of juniper vegetation had slightly higher fire intensities. Also, the fire burned in topography classified as rolling hills with a drainage located in the middle of the area. These higher intensity burn areas removed most of the plant cover and have exposed soils to accelerated soil erosion. These areas are a major concern due to wind and water erosion, the expansion of cheatgrass and noxious weeds.
The Hot Well fire had the best recruitment of sagebrush seedlings that any of the other fire seeded with brush in 2012. The chained junipers at times provided a "catch" for the seed and snow. Multiple sites were found where sagebrush seedlings were growing under chained juniper trees. A seed dribbler was used to aid in the planting of Antelope bitterbrush seed. The area had a large stand of bitterbrush before the burn. The quantitative and qualitative monitoring showed establishment of bitterbrush seedlings. You could follow the dozer track and find seedlings where they had been planted by the dribbler. 
Portions of the lower elevation sites had highest percent cover of annual grasses and noxious weeds. The upper elevation areas had little to no presence of annual grass.
High seed demands from multiple large fires in the District and Great Basin area resulted in an inability to seed sagebrush at the desired rate. Areas with good perennial herbaceous cover will be identified for future planting treatments as funding allows.
2014 monitoring results showed a high increase in annual grasses. It has been observed that the south facing slopes of the second year monitoring on similar fires tend to have a higher amount of annual grass. Also, no Antelope bitterbrush seedlings were observed in 2014 monitoring data. Wildlife tends to be the reason of low survival rate of bitterbrush seedlings. It is my conclusion to continue to monitor for seeding success. Also, the continuation of monitoring for noxious weeds and implementation of eradicating when noxious species are present must also continue.

2021
Quantitative Data
Average density of Wyoming big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata ssp. wyomingensis) over the Wyoming Large Block increased from 0 in 2019 to 0.025 plants/m2 in 2021 (Table 3), but did not meet the objective for seeding success of 0.10 plants/m2. Western yarrow (Achillea millefolium) reached its highest density in 2020, at 0.081 plants/m2, but density of yarrow declined to 0.028 plants/m2 in 2021
Qualitative Data
Wyoming big sagebrush seedlings were observed on only 4 macroplots, and on all but 1 plot where it was common, was present at low cover and considered rare. The seeded western yarrow (Achillea millefolium) was observed on 8 macroplots, and was considered common on 2.

Summary
Three years post-treatment, the Bruneau ESR project area showed variable recovery, with high cover of perennial grasses in some areas, and largely barren areas with cheatgrass thatch in others. Neither of the aerial sagebrush treatments met the objectives for treatment success, but in some locations sagebrush seedlings were observed to be common. It is possible that poor weather conditions during application could have led to variable rates of seed application.
The seed source and seed quality of the aerially seeded sagebrush is unknown, and could have affected success rates. Wyoming big sagebrush seed quality is essential for seeding to be effective. Locally sourced seed that is adapted to the specific microclimate will lead to greater establishment. Since sagebrush seed is relatively short-lived, current year seed is recommended (Meyer and Warren 2015). Sagebrush recruitment is highly weather dependent, with adequate moisture and cool temperatures essential for successful establishment (Meyer 1994). The cool temperatures and above average moisture of 2019 should have helped with sagebrush establishment. Sagebrush seeds are tiny and adversely impacted by competition, especially with aggressive non-native annual grasses. Seeding into dense stands of highly competitive plants such as the thick sward of cheatgrass is generally ineffective (Meyer and Warren 2015). Sagebrush recruitment from seed may also be limited on drier, rocky sites, or sites without microsite heterogeneity that traps snow (such as existing standing live or dead vegetation that is not too dense) (Schuman and Belden 2002, Meyer and Warren 2015).
The ongoing severe drought and warm, windy conditions of 2021 likely caused desiccation and mortality of Wyoming and black sagebrush seedlings that did establish, leading to the lower observed densities of these seeded species in 2021. 

Aerial Seeding- Wyoming big sagebrush area
Three years post-treatment, Wyoming big sagebrush has increased from 0.0083 plants/m\xb2 in 2020 (averaged of 13 macroplots) to 0.025 plants/m\xb2 in 2021. “Eagle” Western Yarrow has decreased from 0.081 plants/m\xb2 in 2020 (averaged of 13 macroplots) to 0.028 plants/m\xb2 in 2021.

FY 17
Monitoring plots were revisited for the 5th year monitoring by Chicago Botanical interns in the summer of 2017. Qualitative assessments were completed and included a general plot description, species inventory, and photo documentation. For the 5th year monitoring year, seven plots were revisited for qualitative assessments. Plots visited include 001, 002, 004, 006, 009, 010, and 012.
The Kinyon Road rehabilitation can be addressed geographically, as the treatments were divided separately into the eastern and western burned areas. The focus of this summary will be on the west side, also known as the Bruneau Overlook area, as heavy noxious weed infestations and unsuccessful drill seedings here were concerning. Due to the good establishment of the drill seed treatments on the eastern side, attention and resources should be focused on the Bruneau Overlook area in future treatments.
On the eastern side of Kinyon, drill seedings were highly successful. Perennial grasses, particularly bluebunch wheatgrass and Siberian wheatgrass, dominate the landscape, and the bare ground among them supports a high diversity of forbs with relatively low cheatgrass establishment. Though sagebrush seedlings were either not found or found in extremely low amounts in these areas, many sagebrush islands were seen near monitoring points, and could potentially re-seed the area regardless of the success of shrub seedings. Invasive weeds such as rush skeletonweed, halogeton, and Russian thistle are present, but are not an imminent threat, especially considering the health and expanse of the perennial grasses. It would be valuable for future projects to assess why the eastern Kinyon plantings were so successful compared to the Bruneau Overlook area.
The Bruneau Overlook seeding treatments have been moderately successful but present several challenges. In some areas, drill-seeded perennial bunchgrass populations are vigorous and extensive with good forb diversity, but cheatgrass density is still high. Most areas on this side of the Kinyon fire are cheatgrass-Sandberg’s bluegrass dominated sites with low forb diversity, and drill-seeded perennials are not competing as well. Few to no sagebrush seedlings were seen across the area, and sagebrush islands were also rarer. Noxious and invasive weed populations also present a problem.
A main concern for this area is extremely dense invasive weed populations, particularly Russian thistle. The Bruneau Overlook area is being overtaken by this dominant weed, and full hillsides of robust Russian thistle were found near monitoring points (Photo 1). The eastern monitoring area also showed some large Russian thistle populations. Russian thistle is likely to continue dominating the Kinyon Road area unless significant control measures are taken. Rush skeletonweed is also present across the Kinyon Road fire area, though to a much lesser extent than the thistle. It has the potential to continue spreading and impeding the advancement of perennial bunchgrasses. Chemical treatments in the Bruneau Overlook area on Russian thistle and rush skeletonweed would be most efficient in stopping the spread of these two species, though mechanical treatments on extremely dense Russian thistle patches could also be valuable.
Kinyon Road Fire (G1CH) FY2022 Monitoring – 10th Year 33
Precipitation data is from the Twin Buttes and Horse Butte RAWS stations, which are northeast of the burned area and southwest of the burned area, respectively. Monitoring reports at the first, second- and third-year mark illuminate a trend towards higher precipitation following treatment years, along with later summer and fall rains. This factor may have contributed to higher weed establishment and lower drill seed success. Previous reports also mention soil movement that filled in drill rows and lessened the establishment rate at Bruneau Overlook sites. Compounding this was the inefficient depth band use on the shrub seedings, consequently the first three years of monitoring found no shrub establishment in the monitoring sites. Upon qualitative monitoring at the five-year mark, scattered immature Wyoming big sagebrush were found in only half of the monitoring sites for all of Kinyon. Multiple factors led to both the low shrub establishment throughout Kinyon and the partial success of drill seed treatments in Bruneau Overlook.

Objectives: To establish a perennial dominated plant community within three years.
Planned_Implementation: Aerially seed grass
Actual_Implementation: This project consisted of aerial seeding 1,500 acres within the Emery fire as part of the Emergency Stabilization Plan. Rate of application was approximately 13.43 pounds bulk seed per acre. The seed was applied to moist and some snow covered ground, see the attached map for the project location. The contractor was Thomas Helicopters, Inc of Gooding, Idaho. The project was completed using one fixed wing plane. The project was started on November 17, 2010 and completed on November 18, 2010.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
FY2011: Of the seeded perennial grass species that were planted over 10% where recorded during the first year of monitoring. Although no forbs were planted, a natural recovery of 13% was observed. Just under half of the cover recorded was bare ground, but with my experience this is common after the first year of a seeding. A little amount of annual grass was documented. This is a good sign that the seeded species will not have much competition with the invasive annual in the next growing seasons.
Four grass species were seeded in the areas that were monitored. The effectiveness of the treatment would be considered successful if the seeded grass species reach densities of 5 -10 plants per square meter. The Two of the four seeded perennial grass species were recorded, and both measured over 5 plants per square meter. Many forbs recovered naturally and at small averages. Some of the larger averages are shown in the table. There was a small presence of cheatgrass in the project area. The next two years of monitoring will be important to show if there are more seeded perennial plants that get recorded and the progress on the plants that were verified in the monitoring.

FY2012: The amount of perennial grass recorded in 2012 increased by a total of 12.60%. Annual grass only increase by 0.45%. All other categories increase by some amount whilst the percentage of bare ground decreased from 2011 to 2012 by 17.2%. During qualitative monitoring, it was noted and recorded that sagebrush seedlings were more abundant from 2011.
A total of five macro-points were monitored in both 2011 and 2012. It was noted in both qualitative and quantitative monitoring that the number of forbs had increased from 2011 to 2012.

FY2013: From the first year of monitoring to the third year the perennial grasses have increased from 10.4% cover to 30% cover. This is a 20% increase over three years. Also, the annual grasses have decreased in cover from 7% to 3% in three years. The cover amount of forbs has also increased from 13.06% in 2011 to 18% in 2013.

It was observed that some of the seeded species were establishing within the harrow and aerial seeded areas, even though they were not detected during monitoring. It is possible that not all seeded species were identifiable during the first two monitoring years; additional time is needed to determine the full outcome of the seeding treatments.

Monitoring Results
Percent Perennial Cover
Line point intercept (LPI) data was used to calculate the percent perennial cover of each AIM monitoring plot. For each AIM plot, the percent foliar cover calculated for each transect was averaged to arrive at an overall percent perennial cover for the plot.

Density
The AIM monitoring crew recorded the number of seeded species and their age class within a 1 meter by 1 meter quadrant every 2.5 meters along a 25 meter transect. The density was calculated by totaling the number of individual plants of every species and age class, and then dividing the total number of plants by 30 sq. meters (3 transects/plot, each contains 10 1x1 meter quadrants) to arrive at the density (plants/sq. meter) of each AIM plot.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The Garat fire (L0LT) burned 9,490 acres; 9,331 acres on BLM-managed land and 159 acres on the Duck Valley Indian Reservation. The Garat fire originated in T14S, R01W, Section 20, SW 1/4, Boise Principal Meridian. Ignition by lightning occurred on July 16, 2018 with containment on July 17 and controlled on July 19. One other documented fire partially burned within the boundary of the current Garat fire; the Yatahoney fire burned 1,102 acres mostly to the north in 2007, 122 acres overlapped with the current fire. No post-fire rehabilitation treatments were implemented on the Yatahoney fire. Multiple other fires have occurred in the area in the past between 1984 and 1985. The Garat 1, Garat 2 and Horse Basin fires consumed 38,970 acres. Fire rehabilitation treatments were implemented on these fires, however no sagebrush seeding treatments were included. The burned area’s elevation ranges from 4,765 to 5,430 feet above sea level. A large bowl referred to as “Jarvis Pasture” on topographic maps runs through the middle of the burned area with plateaus on the north and southwest side. Average annual precipitation in the area ranges from 11 to 13 inches.

As a result of the fire it is expected that there will be an expansion of the annual invasive species that are currently on site, leading to further degradation of desirable site conditions, adversely affecting beneficial wildlife habitat and negatively impacting sage-grouse and other wildlife species. Increased competition from invasive annual grasses and prevent the natural recovery of sagebrush seedlings. Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Aerial Seeding:
The aerial seeding treatment occurred within the Owyhee River Canyon Wilderness Study Area to help maintain land with wilderness characteristics. The 2016 aerial herbicide application, completed the year of the fire in October, was successful in keeping invasive annual grass numbers low, evident in the 2017 photo and Table 7-4. Also, from the same photo there were some perennial plants that survived the fire’s heat. The plants that survived were primarily shallow and deep-rooted bunchgrasses. Bunchgrasses, excluding Sandberg’s bluegrass, had a collective foliar cover of 8%; bluebunch wheatgrass accounted for 7.1% of the total deep rooted perennial bunchgrasses (Tables 7-3 and 7-4). Collectively, the three species of bunchgrass present in 2017 plots had an average density and median diameter of 4.07/m2 and 1.38 inches (Table 7-3). Only the DRPG density objective was met prior to the aerial seeding treatment.
In 2018, plots were revisited after the aerial seeding treatment, completed in December of the previous year. The data displayed in Table 7-3 show an increase for all DRPG measurements (density, diameter, and foliar cover). Both bluebunch wheatgrass and Sandberg’s blue grass increased foliar cover by approximately 3% (Table 7-4) starting the trend in the right direction for meeting the 20% foliar cover objective. The plots completed this year started to detect the encroaching Russian thistle like the drill seeding plots, but the aerial seeding had a lower amount, reflected by the smaller foliar cover of 0.2% (Table 7-4).
In 2019, second year post-treatment, there was a rise in DRPG foliar cover by 10% increasing from 11 to 21% (Table 7-3); coming mostly from bluebunch wheatgrass, a species from the seed mix. Density and median diameter decreased, but that can be due to several factors, like seedlings that did not survive into the second growing season. The objective for density of plants, including seedlings, was still met. The median basal diameter objective has not been achieved over the three years of monitoring data. The noxious weed, Russian thistle, was the dominant herbaceous cover, like what was observed in the drill seeding.
In 2021, third-year post-treatment, the deep-rooted perennial grass foliar cover decreased significantly from the previous down to 13.3% (Table 7-3). With the drop in foliar cover now none of the objectives for the aerial seeding are being met. There is good news, however, in regard to the 11.5% decrease in the cover of the invasive annual, Russian thistle (Figure 7-4).
In 2021, fourth-year post-treatment, the deep-rooted perennial grass foliar cover decreased significantly from the previous down to 13.3% (Table 7-3). With the drop in foliar cover now none of the objectives for the aerial seeding are being met. There is good news, however, regarding the 11.5% decrease in the cover of the invasive annual, Russian thistle (Figure 7-4).

Targeted Control AIM:
In FY 2018 monitoring the natural recovery site there was 0.3% invasive annual grasses, 4.3% deep-rooted
perennial grasses and 23% shallow-rooted bunchgrasses (Table 8-20). The targeted AIM control plot was setup
to provide additional monitoring information that will be used to assess the plot treatment effectiveness and
assist in future land management decisions for the site.

Prior to the fire, lower elevations of the burned area were dominated by Wyoming big
sagebrush and Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda), with some other native bunchgrasses and
cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) present. Upper elevations were dominated by mountain
sagebrush, perennial bunchgrasses, and extensive stands of curl-leaf mountain mahogany
(Cercocarpus ledifolius) which were lost in the fire. Several small stream systems with
riparian vegetation including aspen and willow were impacted by the fire. Scotch thistle
(Onopordum acanthium), a Category B Noxious Weed, and Canada thistle (Cirsium
arvense), a Category C Noxious Weed, are present within the fire perimeter.
Several historical mining structures are within the fire perimeter. The structures were
undamaged by the fire and are unlikely to be impacted by changes that occur because of
the fire.

Without treatment the burned areas are increasingly susceptible to exotic annual dominance; this would jeopardize the 
Greater Sage-Grouse, mule deer herds and other wildlife that depend on this area year-round and especially in the winter 
months. Seeding occurred on sites that do not have the likelihood of naturally recovering from the fire. Areas were seeded 
with perennial species to reduce the dominance of Bromus tectorum.

ESR 2022 Monitoring Report
S3 Aerial Seeding
Goose AIM Plot 01 was correlated to a Shallow Clay Loam 10-14 P.Z. site in a former / Artemisia nova / Pseudoroegneria spicata ssp. spicata ( / black sagebrush / bluebunch wheatgrass ) vegetation site on a hill backslope.
Goose AIM Plot 02 was correlated to a Shallow Loam 8-12 P.Z. site in a former / Artemisia tridentata ssp. wyomingensis / Achnatherum thurberianum – Pseudoroegneria spicata ( / Wyoming big sagebrush / Thurber’s needlegrass – Bluebunch wheatgrass) vegetation site on a hill backslope.
Goose AIM Plot 03A was correlated to a Loamy Bottom 8-14 P.Z. site in a former / Artemisia tridentata ssp. tridentata / Leymus cinereus ( / basin big sagebrush / basin wildrye) vegetation site on a floodplain.
Goose 01, Goose 02, and Goose 03A were all treated with the Aerial Seeding mix which was comprised of Snake River wheatgrass (Elymus wawawaiensis), Great Basin wildrye (Leymus cinereus), Thickspike wheatgrass (Elymus lanceolatus), Sherman bluegrass(Poa secunda), Alfalfa (Medicago sativa), Wyoming big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata ssp wyomingensis), and Mountain big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata ssp vaseyana).
In 2022, Goose 03A was determined to a plot that should have been rejected due to a stream flowing through the entirety of the plot. Therefore, it was not surveyed in 2022 and will not be surveyed again in the future.
2020: The monitoring objectives for the seeding was 3 seeded bunchgrasses, 1 native forb, and 0.3 shrubs per square meter. Grasses and forbs met objectives on AIM Plot 01, some grasses and forbs were observed through density on AIM Plot 02, and no seeded species were observed in density on AIM Plot 03. Seeded species were observed in all three plots’ species inventory. Recovery of grasses is going well on all three sites and the majority of the recovery is from Poa species.
2021: The monitoring objectives for each of the sites was not met. Seeded bunchgrasses were met for Goose 01, native regrowth of forbs and shrubs were observed on the plots and cumulatively met the goal of more than 1 forb/m2 and 0.3 shrubs/m2 but no other objectives were met for any of the 3 plots. Overall, there was a decline in total density of plant species across all three plots.
2022: The rehabilitation objectives for this site were not met due to the continued lack of seeded sagebrush being present on the plots. No seed shrubs or seeded forbs were observed while grass species, both seeded and native regrowth, are observed in strong numbers. However, native regrowth of shrubs is showing continued signs of establishment and stabilization on the plots.
AIM Data Results:
Cover
2020: Average foliar canopy cover was moderate (59.3%) with cheatgrass and an unknown perennial grass taking the highest cover (10.4% and 10.2%, respectively). All combined perennial species had much higher cover (57.5%) than the combined cover for all annual species observed in LPI (29.9%). Many of the sites had a diversity of grass species and some tree cover.
2021: Average foliar canopy cover decreased from 2020 by 12.63% (46.67%), with large drops in perennial grasses and both perennial and annual forbs (-19% and -6%/-13% respectively). The only indicator that had an increase in foliar cover was trees with an increase of 2% since 2020.
2022: Average foliar cover increased significantly from 46.67% in 2021 to 71.7T% with annual forbs taking over as the most dominant on the plot with 29.6% cover. The next abundant indicator were perennial grasses at 16.5, a decrease of 10% since last year, all other indicators saw decreases as well.
Gaps and Erosion
2020: Gaps occurred mostly in >200cm segments and occupied 18.8% of the average 25m transects.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: The Buckskin Fire started on 9/15/2011 by lightning and was contained on 9/17/2011 after burning a total of 2,000 acres. The fire burned in the Tule Springs Pasture of the Tule Springs Allotment # 6018.There are no Wilderness Study Areas or Wilderness associated with the burned area, however the burn is within the Alvord-Tule Wild Horse Herd Management Area. Vegetation within the burned area was dominated by Wyoming big sagebrush with a significant understory of introduced annual grasses (cheatgrass and Japanese brome).  The Tule Springs area is one of the driest portions of the Burns District receiving only 6 to 8 inches of precipitation annually.  A number of fires have burned in the Tuley Springs area since the early 1980s,  Post-fire plant communities often resulted in large areas of exposed soils subject to wind erosion.  Since the late 1990s, seeding( both aerial and drill) has occurred on most fires with fairly good success.  Seeding has proven to limit soil movement and helped to limit dominance to invasive annual plants.  The Buckskin Fire will be aerial seeded with perennial species (Wyoming big sagebrush and forage kochia) to control and prevent short-term soil loss and cheatgrass and other invasive annuals from dominating the site. The proposed seeding in the Buckskin fire area is fenced separately from the rest of the allotment in the Tule Springs pasture  Herders provided by the grazing permittee would move any cattle that wander into the area, away from the proposed seeding. There should not be much pressure from livestock in this area, because available livestock water can be controlled by turning on or turning off  water to troughs on the existing pipeline in the area. The 2,000 acre seeding would be a small part of the 136,895 acre Tule Spring Pasture; therefore, temporary fencing, which would increase the rehabilitation cost unnecessarily, and is not proposed for this burned area. This method of protection has been used in the past in this general area, with success.

Planned_Implementation: All BLM burned acres will be aerial seeded utilizing a combination of two separate seeds mixes. Approximately, 4,500 acres in the Badger fire would be aerially seeded with a native seed mix (Greater Sage-Grouse Areas) and an additional 9,000 acres will be aerial seeded with native like seed mix (Steep Slopes, Drainages and Low Elevation) in the fall of 2020.
Actual_Implementation: This project consisted of aerial seeding 13,551 acres of the Badger Fire prior to chaining the areas accessible to dozers. The contractor was Crop Jet Aviation, LLC out of Gooding, Idaho. The project was completed using three fixed wing aircraft. The grass and forb seed were premixed by ESR staff. The project was started on October 16th and completed on October 23, 2020. During the time there was a cold front that lasted for six days, with high winds.\r\nThere were two seed mixes for the project. The mix seeded on the chaining area, 4,598 acres, was a native mix called Sage Grouse. The mix for the remaining area, 8,953 acres, was a non-native mix called Slopes.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Sage Grouse (Native) Seed Mix 

Two years post-treatment the total density of seeded grass species from the Sage Grouse (native) seed mix was 0.81 plants/m2, which does not meet the treatment objective (Table 6). Bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata) was the dominant seeded grass species in terms of density and cover, with squirreltail (Elymus elymoides) and Sherman’s big bluegrass (Poa secunda ‘sherman’) also present (Tables 5-6). Seeded forbs did not meet density objective, with a total density of 0.10 plants/m2 (Table 6) and no seeded forbs recorded on cover-point transects (Table 5). However, total cover and density of non-seeded forbs was very high in 2022 (Tables 5-6), likely due to the wet spring. Cover and density of non-seeded grasses were also much higher in 2022, with grass cover almost doubling from 2021 levels (Table 5-6). Bitterbrush (Purshia tridentata) was not observed on monitoring transects (Tables 5-6). Cover and density of cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) was higher in 2022 than in 2021, but still relatively low on Sage Grouse seed mix monitoring plots (Tables 5-6). Noxious weeds were not recorded on monitoring transects in either year (Tables 5-6).

Three years post-treatment the total density of seeded grass species from the Sage Grouse (native) seed mix was 2.13 plants/m2, a significant increase from the 0.81 plants/m2 recorded in 2022 (Table 6), but below the treatment objective of 3.0 plants/m2. Bluebunch wheatgrass was the dominant seeded grass species in terms of density and cover, with squirreltail the only other seeded grass species on cover and density transects in 2023 (Tables 5-6). Other grasses, predominately Sandberg bluegrass, accounted for most of the perennial grass density and cover on Sage Grouse seed treatment plots (Tables 5-6). Seeded forbs did not meet density objective, with a total density of 0.14 plants/m2 (Table 6) and no seeded forbs were recorded on cover transects (Table 5). However, total cover and density of non-seeded forbs remained high in 2023, although both declined from 2022 due to much lower annual forb abundance in the drier conditions of 2023 (Tables 5-6). Bitterbrush was not observed on cover or density transects, but density of other shrubs increased in 2023 (Tables 5-6). Cover and density of cheatgrass increased significantly, with density increasing from 22.77 plants/m2 in 2022 to 130.43 plants/m2 in 2023 (Tables 5-6). Noxious weeds were not recorded on monitoring transects in 2023 (Tables 5-6).

Slopes (Non-native) seed mix 

Two years post-treatment, the total density of seeded grass species from the Slopes (non-native) seed mix was 1.86 plants/m2, which does not meet the treatment objective (Table 9). Siberian wheatgrass (Agropyron fragile) was the dominant seeded grass species in terms of density and cover, with Snake River wheatgrass (Elymus wawawaiensis) also present (Tables 8-9). Bitterbrush was not observed on monitoring transects (Tables 8-9). Other forbs increased in cover and especially density, with density increasing from 5.93 plants/m2 in 2021 to 114.16 plants/m2 between 2021 and 2022 (Tables 8-9). Other grasses also increased significantly in terms of cover and density between 2021 and 2022 (Tables 8-9), with bluebunch wheatgrass and Sandberg bluegrass dominant other grass species.  As with the Sage Grouse seeded area, cover and density of cheatgrass was higher in 2022 than in 2021, but still relatively low (Tables 8-9). Noxious weeds were not recorded on monitoring transects in either monitoring year (Tables 8-9).

Three years post-treatment, the total density of seeded grass species from the Slopes (non-native) seed mix was 1.36 plants/m2, a decline from 1.86 plants/m2 in 2022, and below the treatment objective (Table 9). Siberian wheatgrass was the dominant seeded grass species in terms of density and cover, with Snake River wheatgrass also present (Tables 8-9). Other grasses comprised the majority of cover and density, but declined from 2022 to 2023 (Tables 8-9). Sandberg bluegrass was the dominant species in terms of cover and density, with bluebunch wheatgrass also significant, and smaller contributions from crested wheatgrass and squirreltail. Bitterbrush was not observed on monitoring transects (Tables 8-9). Other forbs decreased in cover and density from 2022 to 2023, but remained an important component of the vegetation community (Tables 8-9). As with the Sage Grouse seeded area, cheatgrass abundance was higher in 2023 than in 2022, with density increasing from 16.27 plants/m2 to 125.58 plants/m2 in 2023 (Tables 8-9).
